articles.title: British man charged in Singapore two years after alleged theft at Changi airport
articles.summary: The 26-year-old faces up to seven years in jail for allegedly stealing a denim jacket from an airport shop in 2024.
articles.body:
Singapore has charged a British man for theft more than two years after he allegedly stole a denim jacket from a store at the airport shopping mall.

The police were alerted to the theft in the evening of 14 August 2024 when a retail assistant at Singapore's Changi Airport realised a blue denim jacket was missing from a display mannequin.

Surveillance footage showed a man removing the jacket, worth about S$350 ($275; £202), from the mannequin and leaving the store without making payment. By the time the authorities established his identity, the man had departed Singapore.

The 26-year-old was arrested on 15 August this year while in transit at the airport and was charged on Tuesday.

"The police take a serious stance of shop theft and will deal firmly with offenders in accordance with the law.

"Offenders should not assume that they can evade detection simply by leaving Singapore after committing an offence," the Singapore Police Force said in a statement on Monday.

In its statement the police also recounted a separate arrest of a 50-year-old Polish woman who had stolen two bottles of perfume from retail stores inside one of the airport's terminals on 11 June this year.

She was arrested in the transit area shortly before she was scheduled to depart Singapore. The woman was charged with two counts of theft on Tuesday.

Those convicted of theft in Singapore face up to seven years in jail.

articles.title: Deportees who refused to exit a U.S. flight in Liberia are sent to Equatorial Guinea
articles.summary: The six people from Cuba, Brazil and Cameroon were flown to another African nation as part of a third-country deportation deal with the Trump administration.
articles.body: DAKAR, Senegal — Six people who were deported by the United States to Liberia last week resisted getting off the plane and instead were sent to Equatorial Guinea, another African nation that signed a third-country deportation agreement with the Trump administration, a person on the plane and a lawyer in contact with the six said Monday. Under a series of often secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to two dozen countries that aren’t their own as it pushes ahead with its immigration crackdown, advocates say. Immigration lawyers say the practice is being used as a legal loophole to indirectly return some asylum seekers to countries they fled. The people who refused to get off the plane in Liberia on Thursday were four Cuban men, a Brazilian man and a Cameroonian woman, the person and the lawyer said. A Honduran deportee aboard the flight said the group refused to disembark, saying Liberia was “not their country” and that they would face danger there. They were then separated from the others, he said. He spoke on condition of anonymity out of fear of reprisals. He said the other passengers got off in Liberia because they feared officers would force them. Meredyth Yoon, litigation director for Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta, said the deportees who resisted leaving the plane in Liberia were told they would be returned to the United States but instead were flown to Malabo city in Equatorial Guinea. “It was a really heartbreaking and chaotic scene when they arrived in Malabo on Thursday,” Yoon said. Some arrived in chains and in extreme distress, she said, including the Cameroonian woman and one of the Cuban men, who Yoon said has a large abdominal growth and uses a colostomy bag that must be drained regularly. There is no medical staff at the hotel in Equatorial Guinea where the six are being held, alongside around 40 other deported migrants, she added. Conditions at the hotel have worsened in recent months, Yoon said, with food sometimes withheld and guards accused of threatening, beating and choking some of the migrants. Equatorial Guinea’s government did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Under an opaque $7.5 million deal with the Trump administration, Equatorial Guinea’s all-powerful president, Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, has turned the hotel owned by his family into a prison for asylum seekers deported from the U.S. One of the Cubans sent to Equatorial Guinea was Carlos Rodríguez López, 35, who had been living in Miami Gardens, Florida. Igrayne Ribot, his wife and the mother of their daughter, said in an interview with the Telemundo affiliate in Miami that news of her husband’s deportation “arrived all of a sudden.” After receiving a notification about her husband’s transfer, she was able to reach him via video call. He told her he was in Africa. “I broke down,” she said. “Nobody imagines something like that — it was terrifying.”

articles.title: In 2009, Iceland drillers hit 1,000°C magma by accident, unlocking a geothermal source that could produce nearly 10 times more power
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2009, a drilling operation in northeast Iceland unexpectedly punched into molten rock at Krafla, revealing one of the hottest geothermal resources .
articles.body: In 2009, a drilling operation in northeast Iceland unexpectedly punched into molten rock at Krafla, revealing one of the hottest geothermal resources ever reached by a borehole. The Iceland Deep Drilling Project(IDDP) had been searching for high-temperature geothermal energy, but instead of finding only hot water and rock, the drill encountered magma at about 2.1 kilometres below the surface. Temperatures there were estimated at roughly 900–1,000°C. What followed turned an accident into an extraordinary energy experiment. Engineers managed to complete the well and draw superheated steam from the area around the magma, showing that heat close to molten rock could deliver far more energy than geothermal wells. The result also gave scientists a unique glimpse into a part of Earth that is almost impossible to reach, setting the stage for a more ambitious attempt to study and use magma.1000°C magma encounter become an energy experimentInstead of simply abandoning the well, the project team decided to find out what the unexpected magma encounter could actually do. The engineers installed a steel casing in the well, with the lower section perforated near the magma. The hole was then allowed to heat gradually. Eventually, it began producing extremely hot, high-pressure steam. IDDP-1 produced superheated steam for roughly two years, until July 2012. During testing, the steam reached temperatures above 450°C, making the well the hottest geothermal production well in the world at the time. The steam could also be fed directly into the existing Krafla power plant. The result was much more significant than setting a temperature record. It demonstrated that a geothermal well could operate extremely close to molten rock and draw useful energy from the intense heat surrounding it.What was the drilling team looking for in IcelandThe team was searching for a better source of geothermal energy. The IDDP was established to investigate whether extremely hot underground conditions could provide much more energy than conventional geothermal systems. At Krafla, in northeast Iceland, the project planned to drill far deeper than the point where most geothermal wells normally operate. According to PhysOrg, IDDP-1 was intended to explore high-temperature resources, with the original drilling programme taking the well towards depths of around 4.5 kilometres. Instead, the drill encountered something completely unexpected at just 2.1 kilometres which was molten rock with temperatures of approximately 900–1,000°C. The discovery was extraordinary because drilling directly into magma is extremely rare. Therefore, Krafla became a natural laboratory where scientists could study what happens when a well reaches the boundary between solid rock and molten material.Why was the well so much more powerfulThe reason was the enormous amount of heat available at such extreme temperatures. Conventional geothermal wells generally rely on naturally heated underground water. Superhot geothermal systems aim to reach much hotter conditions, where water carries substantially more energy. The ‘Clean Air Task Force’ reported that IDDP-1 could have generated up to 36 megawatts of electricity, equivalent to roughly 5-10 times the output of a typical commercial geothermal well operating at lower temperatures. It also described the well as the world's hottest production well when it reached 450°C during operation. The reason is relatively simple that when ‘water is subjected to extreme underground heat, it can become superheated steam capable of carrying far more energy to the surface.’ That is why the accidental discovery became so important. The drill had not simply found hot rock; it had revealed a potentially much more energy-dense geothermal resource.Challenges created by the extreme heat inside the wellThe same conditions that made IDDP-1 powerful also made it incredibly difficult to operate. The ‘Clean Air Task Force’ noted that the project faced severe corrosion while the well was heating up. The casing also had to withstand exceptionally hostile temperatures and fluids. Once the fluid became sufficiently hot, however, corrosion decreased substantially. The experience showed engineers that future wells would need carefully designed casings, valves, cement and surface equipment capable of surviving these conditions.The project also faced mechanical setbacks. According to AAPG, the drill became stuck and the team had to sidetrack the well during the effort. The experience nevertheless produced valuable information about drilling through extremely hot and pressurised underground environments. Eventually, IDDP-1 was shut down in 2012 after problems with surface equipment. But the experiment had already proved its central point that extremely hot geothermal resources could potentially produce dramatically more electricity from a single well.Foundation of the Krafla Magma Testbed(KMT)The unexpected discovery did not end with the IDDP-1 experiment. Instead, it inspired a much larger scientific ambition. The Krafla Magma Testbed (KMT) was developed as an international project designed to create the world's first magma observatory. Its aim is to deliberately access magma at Krafla and study it directly rather than waiting for another accidental encounter. KMT says the site is particularly valuable because a known magma body exists at relatively shallow depth, making Krafla an exceptional place for controlled research.The ‘International Continental Scientific Drilling Program’ states that rhyolitic magma at Krafla is known to exist at roughly 2.1–2.5 kilometres depth and around 900°C. Researchers hope to examine the boundary between the magma and surrounding rock, while also keeping the well available for long-term observations. The planned work is about more than electricity. Scientists want to understand how heat and fluids move around magma, improve instruments that can survive extreme underground conditions and learn more about volcanic systems.Could magma become a new source of geothermal powerThe Krafla experience suggests that it could, although major engineering challenges remain. KMT describes superhot geothermal resources as having the potential to greatly increase energy output per well. The project is being developed as both a research facility and a testbed for technologies that could eventually make these resources easier and safer to utilise. The AGU report also noted that KMT could help researchers understand how heat moves from magma into the surrounding geothermal system. One earlier analysis suggested that long-term flows of superheated steam from the IDDP-1 area could potentially produce more than 30 megawatts of electricity from a single well. The accidental drilling of 2009 ultimately changed the direction of geothermal research. Today, the goal is no longer to avoid magma. Scientists and engineers are increasingly asking whether, with the right technology, they can safely reach it, understand it and perhaps one day turn its extraordinary heat into a dependable source of clean electricity.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: BPSC exam row, 'dogs bark' remark: What has triggered fresh student protests in Bihar
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Chaotic scenes unfolded in Biharâs Patna on Tuesday as protesting students clashed with police during a massive protest over alleged irregu.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Chaotic scenes unfolded in Biharâs Patna on Tuesday as protesting students clashed with police during a massive protest over alleged irregularities in the 70th BPSC examination.The protest was met with a heavy police deployment, with barricades erected to stop the students from marching.Police also used water cannons as protesters attempted to push past the barricades.Later, the Samrat Choudhary-led government claimed it had addressed âalmost all issuesâ raised by the students. The protesters, however, said several long-standing demands remained unresolved and continued their agitation.The students marched from Gandhi Maidan towards Raj Bhavan.The protesting students also broke the barricades in bid to gherao chief minister's residence.The protest has also brought into focus delays in recruitment examinations, the proposed format of the Teacher Recruitment Examination-4 (TRE-4), alleged paper leaks and demands for greater transparency in Bihar's recruitment system.Govt says students' issues have been addressedBihar education minister Mithilesh Tiwari said the government had resolved the issues raised by the students and maintained that its doors remained open for further dialogue."All the issues over which the students were staging a sit-in have been resolved. It is not as if the student agitation was the sole reason for this; it is the government's very intent to resolve the problems faced by our youth in a timely manner. We have addressed every issue raised by the youth. I was surprised to hear a person who has never even taken a board exam offering suggestions on examinations. That is why I would say to Tejashwi Yadav to enroll in a Bihar government school, pass the tenth-grade exam, and then come back to offer us suggestions on examinations," Tiwari said.The minister said that almost all the demands had been met and invited students to approach the government with any remaining concerns."We have met almost all the students' demands. For any students who wish to convey further points to the government, the doors for dialogue remain wide open. Let the students come, talk, and get their issues resolved; the government belongs to them," he said.However, the protesters said their concerns had not been fully addressed and that problems related to the education system, examination paper leaks and delayed recruitment continued.'Do you need 1,800 years?' Students question recruitment delaysProtester Vikas Bhatt said the students were demanding improvements in Bihar's education system and action against repeated examination paper leaks."Our demand is that the education system in Bihar be improved. We are raising issues regarding the frequent exam paper leaks in the state. Look at the recruitment for librarians, it hasn't happened for 18 years; do you need 1,800 years? Whenever we stage a protest, they simply offer assurances and leave it at that. How can things go on like this? Three recruitment drives were announced through the BSSC, but it has been three years. We have repeatedly besieged the BSSC commission, demanding that the exam dates be announced. Despite this, they keep asking for 15 days' time. Apart from the BPSC, there isn't a single commission in Bihar that issues an annual calendar," Bhatt said.The students are demanding the cancellation of the 70th BPSC examination over allegations of irregularities and paper leaks.The agitation has also centred on the proposed TRE-4 examination. Students have opposed the proposal to conduct the examination in two phases across Bihar and are demanding that it be held in a single phase.They have also sought the immediate release of the official TRE-4 advertisement.Students break through barricades during Raj Bhavan marchAs the protest continued, students marched from Gandhi Maidan towards Raj Bhavan. Some protesters broke through police barricades and attempted to move towards the restricted area.Police used water cannons to disperse the crowd, while several protesters were detained.DSP Kamakhya Narayan Singh said the police would not allow the protesters to enter the restricted area, although he expressed hope that the ongoing talks between students and senior officials would lead to a resolution."We will stop them; we won't let them proceed further. However, the dialogue has been positive, and we hope the students will agree. They have raised several issues with the senior officials, and the outcome has been positive. So, I expect the turnout to be lower and that they will agree. If they don't, we will stop them right here. We won't allow them to enter the restricted area," Singh said.Congress leader Sushil Kumar, who was present at the protest site, said the government had failed to give assurances on several key demands."We want to state clearly that a single-stage examination must be implemented for TRE 4.0 at all costs, and negative marking should be abolished. There are numerous other issues as well, regarding the BPSC, BSSC, Sub-Inspector recruitment. The government has offered no assurances on any of these points. We have urged the Chief Minister to hold a dialogue; he should invite our delegation for talks. We have been on a hunger strike for nine days, yet no one is willing to listen to us. Just imagine, had the government engaged in dialogue, this situation would not have arisen. We are heading towards the Chief Minister's residence; the Chief Minister should hold talks, and our delegation will go there for the discussion," Kumar told news agency ANI.JD(U) says govt is serious about students' concernsJD(U) leader Shravan Kumar said the Bihar government was taking the concerns of students and job seekers seriously and was acting according to established rules and legal provisions."The government is taking the demands and concerns of students and job seekers seriously. Everything is being done for them in accordance with established rules, laws, and provisions. Bihar is the first state in the country to have made such large-scale recruitments across government departments," Kumar said.He also pointed to the government's employment target for the 2025-2030 period and urged young people not to be influenced by the opposition."It is Nitish Kumar's resolve to provide 10 million (1 crore) jobs and employment opportunities to the people of Bihar between 2025 and 2030. Recruitments are taking place in every sector, and vacancies are being announced in every department. I urge our youth to exercise patience and not fall for the opposition's ploys; they are not going to provide jobs. They merely intend to exploit your hard work and sweat to further their own political interests. Beware of them," he added.Tejashwi writes to Samrat ChoudharyMeanwhile, Bihar leader of opposition Tejashwi Yadav has written to chief minister Samrat Choudhary over the ongoing BPSC row, urging the government not to ignore the students' demands and to hold talks for an early resolution.Tejashwi has demanded that TRE-4 be conducted as a single examination across the state. He has also sought an end to what he described as discrimination against Hindi-speaking candidates in the BPSC Civil Services Main Examination and interview.The RJD leader has further demanded complete transparency in all competitive examinations, including those for Sub-Inspector, Constable, BSSC and BPSC recruitments.Among his other demands are a high-level independent inquiry into alleged irregularities in past examinations, strict action against recruitment mafias and time-bound schedules for all pending tests.He has specifically called for clear timelines for the BSSC Intermediate, CGL, ASO, BSO, Librarian and Accountant recruitment examinations.RJD scion Tejashwi remark also followed BPSC official's "dog-barking" remark. Bihar LoP also called for action for his remark referring to students.Bihar launches monthly student support campsAmid the continuing protests, the Bihar government on Tuesday launched the monthly 'Vidyarthi Sahyog Shivir' or student support camps to address students' grievances.The camps will be organised at educational institutions on the fourth Tuesday of every month, chief minister Samrat Choudhary said in a social media post."The Bihar government is launching Vidyarthi Sahyog Shivir starting today to ensure prompt resolution of students' grievances. These camps will be organised at educational institutions on the fourth Tuesday of every month," Choudhary wrote.The camps will allow students to raise their grievances directly with the concerned government officials. Students will also be able to register complaints online and track their status through the portal and Helpline 1100.The government's announcement comes as the student protest continues in Patna's Gardanibagh area, with the two sides offering sharply different views on whether the protesters' demands have been addressed.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Family of Alex Pretti speaks out in exclusive interview: 'They murdered our child'
articles.summary: Pretti was shot and killed by federal officers on Jan. 24.
articles.body:
Seven months after 37-year-old Alex Pretti was shot and killed by two federal immigration officers in Minneapolis, his grieving family said they want "accountability" in their first television interview.

"We've seen what happened. The videos are pretty clear. But we want justice. We want accountability for the people that did this to Alex," his father, Michael Pretti, said in the exclusive interview with "Good Morning America" co-anchor George Stephanopoulos while joined by his wife and daughter.

Alex Pretti , an American citizen and ICU nurse for the Department of Veterans Affairs, was killed on Jan. 24, roughly two weeks after fellow U.S. citizen Renee Good was shot and killed by an ICE officer in Minneapolis during the Trump administration's "Operation Metro Surge" immigration crackdown. Both shootings sparked nationwide outrage and demands for accountability over federal officers' deadly use of force in Minneapolis.

Michael Pretti said his son was observing immigration activity when the shooting occurred.

"He cared deeply about his community. Minneapolis was his community. He wanted people to be treated fairly, no matter what walk of life, what their background was," Michael Pretti said.

Watch the interview with the Prettis and George Stephanopoulos on "Good Morning America," airing Tuesday, Aug. 25, at 7 a.m.

Eyewitness video shows that Alex Pretti appeared to be recording when a federal officer shoves a woman into him. He seems to try to help her, and then both of his hands are visible -- one holding a phone and the other held up, seemingly to protect himself from pepper spray -- when he's wrestled to the ground. His firearm, which he had a legal permit to carry, was removed by an officer while he was on the ground and before approximately 10 shots were fired, the video shows.

A minute-by-minute timeline of the fatal shooting of Alex Pretti involving federal agents

His parents said they found out their son had been shot while watching the coverage of the shooting on the news. His mother said she recognized her son's jacket and sunglasses from the footage.

"That's how we found out, watching it on TV. Watching our son be shot ten times on TV," Michael Pretti said.

"In the back," Susan Pretti, Alex's mother, added.

"I was not shocked that he helped somebody. My shock is that he was murdered and no one has given us the complete truth or anyone has been held accountable. And it's been seven months," Susan Pretti said.

"What did he do to deserve to be murdered? To be left cold, on the ground, dead, my child? What did he do?" she asked.

In the wake of the deadly shooting, some Trump administration officials were quick to blame Alex Pretti. Former Border Patrol Commander Greg Bovino said it looked like Pretti wanted "to do maximum damage and massacre law enforcement," and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem claimed he "committed an act of domestic terrorism."

Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller posted on social media that he was an "assassin" and "domestic terrorist."

When asked about the response, Michael Pretti said, "There was more effort in vilifying him than pursuing justice, investigating this."

After video of him in a confrontation with federal agents 11 days before the shooting surfaced on social media, President Donald Trump called Alex Pretti an "agitator" and "perhaps" an "insurrectionist" in a social media post.

Asked what it felt like to hear those things said about their family member, his sister, Micayla Pretti, said, "I don't think you would like my answer."

"It's so un-presidential," Michael Pretti said. "It's ridiculous that, you know, the leader of the free world speaks that way about an American citizen."

Susan Pretti said she wants an apology for what was said about her son. "Why shouldn't we get one?" she asked.

The Department of Justice opened a federal civil rights investigation into the shooting. Steve Schleicher, an attorney for the Pretti family, told ABC News that they don't know where that stands or what information they've gathered.

"They at least have the right to know who shot Alex Pretti," Schleicher said. "They have the right to be consulted with meaningfully, they have the right to meet with the prosecutors, they have the right to have the process not drag on too long. They have the right to be informed, and that's just not being done here."

In a letter to then-Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche last month, Schleicher said that the U.S. attorney in Minnesota met with the Pretti family on July 13 but that "the meeting raised more questions than answers."

2nd Amendment backlash follows portrayal of Alex Pretti by some Trump administration officials

A DOJ spokesperson said in a statement to ABC News, "As is standard protocol, family member communications, if any, come at a later stage of a case, such as at indictment, initial appearance, plea, trial, or sentencing. Communications with family do not typically occur during an investigation."

The Department of Homeland Security and FBI are also involved in the investigation, the DOJ said. A DHS spokesperson told ABC News that the investigation remains active, while the FBI declined to comment.

ABC News asked the White House if Trump and Stephen Miller still stand by what they said about Alex Pretti, but they did not answer the question.

A DHS spokesperson said the agency "works to give the American people accurate information as quickly as possible. These statements were made based on information received on the ground from CBP."

"This is a law enforcement matter and an active investigation and we refer you to FBI for further questions. We urge individuals not to impede any law enforcement action and ICE operations," the spokesperson said.

Asked what justice looks like for them, Micayla Pretti said she wants the names of the agents who shot her brother officially released.

"They murdered our child," Susan Pretti said. "People need to be held responsible when they murder people in this country. Period."

articles.title: Rajnath Singh approves transfer of DRDO missile technology to Indian defence industry
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh has approved the transfer of DRDO-developed technologies for all conventional missile systems to Indian defe.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh has approved the transfer of DRDO-developed technologies for all conventional missile systems to Indian defence companies for production within the country, the defence ministry said on Tuesday.The move is aimed at accelerating indigenous missile manufacturing, reducing import dependence and expanding the role of domestic companies in India's defence ecosystem.The ministry described the technology transfer as an "important milestone" in increasing industry participation and enabling the transition of missile systems from development to industrial production."The provision will enable successful transition of missile system development to industrial production, reflecting the continued efforts of DRDO (Defence Research and Development Organisation) to leverage the capabilities of the Indian industry for the development and manufacture of advanced defence systems," the ministry said.Under the initiative, Indian defence companies will be able to undertake production of DRDO-developed conventional missile technologies, subject to applicable qualifications, certifications and regulatory requirements.The government said the move is intended to strengthen India's domestic defence industrial base and expand manufacturing capabilities.The initiative will also create opportunities for Indian micro, small and medium enterprises and other technology partners to participate in missile production and related supply chains.The defence ministry said the initiative would increase domestic value addition while supporting the growth of India's defence manufacturing sector.DRDO will continue to work with Indian industry to facilitate the transfer and absorption of advanced defence technologies, the ministry said.

articles.title: Who are Iran’s top trading partners US would need to target to isolate it?
articles.summary: The US wants to isolate Iran from the global economy. Here is who Tehran trades with, and how much is at stake.
articles.body:
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has unveiled a new wave of sanctions on Iran, branded “Operation Economic Outcast”, designating close to 60 entities, individuals and vessels and widening secondary sanctions to cover shipping, gold, aviation, technology and digital assets.

He said the aim was to sever every economic lifeline sustaining the government in Tehran until it stands alone, and that President Donald Trump was telephoning world leaders with specific requests to halt their dealings with Iran, though he named no countries and set no deadline.

Below, we break down Iran’s top trading partners using official customs figures compiled by Trade Data Monitor, which exclude the unrecorded flows sustaining much of Iran’s oil exports.

Iran has spent much of the past two decades under Western sanctions, a pressure that has pushed its economy away from Europe and towards a narrowing group of Asian and regional partners.

In 2024, Iran exported some $56bn worth of goods to at least 112 countries and territories, according to official customs figures. Its top export partners were:

China ($14.58bn) – The largest buyer of Iranian oil, taking more than 80 percent of Iran’s seaborne crude exports, according to tanker-tracking analysts. Much of it is discounted and moved by shadow-fleet vessels, barely registering in either country’s customs records.

Iraq ($11.7bn) – Iran has been a major supplier of gas to Iraq for electricity generation, and sells electricity directly to Iraqi provinces in the south. It is also a leading source of food products, building materials and manufactured goods.

UAE ($7.16bn) – Has long been a financial and re-export lifeline for Iran, accounting for 13 percent of its exports. Abu Dhabi imposed an indefinite trade embargo last week after accusing Iran of firing missiles at its territory. Tehran denied the allegations.

Turkiye ($6.1bn) – Iran has long supplied Turkiye with pipeline gas via the Tabriz-Ankara Pipeline, along with petrochemicals, food products, and construction materials.

Afghanistan ($2.3bn) Iran supplies its landlocked neighbour with fuel, food and construction materials, and Afghanistan depends heavily on Iranian ports and overland routes to access wider markets.

In 2024, Iran imported some $68.5bn worth of goods from at least 87 countries and territories, according to official customs figures. Its top import partners were:

UAE ($21bn) – Supplied just above 30 percent of Iran’s imports, most of them re-exported goods rather than Emirati production, giving Tehran indirect access to Western machinery, electronics and consumer goods. Abu Dhabi’s indefinite trade embargo has severed that route.

China ($17.8bn) – The main supplier of machinery, electronics, vehicles and industrial components, and the partner Iran has leaned on most heavily as Western trade has closed off.

Turkiye ($11.1bn) – A shared land border and longstanding commercial ties make Turkiye a key overland supply route, sending machinery, chemicals, vehicles and manufactured goods. Trade in both directions has fallen since the war began.

European Union ($6.1bn) – European sales are now a fraction of pre-2018 levels, concentrated in pharmaceuticals, medical equipment and machinery.

India ($1.6bn) – Trade has fallen sharply in recent years. New Delhi has kept commercial links narrow and weighted towards agricultural goods including rice, tea and pharmaceuticals.

articles.title: U.S. cancels South Korea marine drills over tied up forces in Iran war
articles.summary: The United States cancelled a joint amphibious landing drill scheduled for next month with South Korea, Seoul’s Marine Corps said on Monday, after Washington cited constraints on the availability of U.S. forces due to the war in Iran.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — The United States canceled a joint amphibious landing drill scheduled for next month with South Korea, Seoul’s Marine Corps said Monday, after Washington cited constraints on the availability of U.S. forces due to the war in Iran. The U.S. Marine Corps formally notified its South Korean counterpart in June that force availability would be constrained for the division-level exercise, known as Ssangyong, a South Korean Marine Corps spokesperson told a news briefing. The allies remain in close consultations on resuming the drills, the spokesperson said. He did not specify what measures might be taken to prevent future cancellations or to make up for lost training opportunities. U.S. Forces Korea did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Later on Monday, the U.S. State Department said that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had spoken with South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun about a “range of issues” in their alliance. Rubio told his South Korean counterpart that Washington and Seoul need to remain in close coordination on matters integral to their alliance, according to a State Department statement. The cancellation of the amphibious landing drill follows President Donald Trump’s surprise order to scale back a separate annual joint military exercise that ended last Friday, citing the cost and Seoul’s refusal to take part in the Iran war. North Korea — whose leader, Kim Jong Un, Trump has repeatedly expressed interest in meeting again — has long condemned such joint exercises as rehearsals for invasion. Referring to North Korea, Trump also wrote on his Truth Social platform that the Ulchi Freedom Shield drills sent “a signal that was totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful.” Despite the reduction of the exercises, Pyongyang fired 10 short-range ballistic missiles last week and issued a statement denouncing the exercises.

articles.title: Kremlin adviser warns UK drone factories could face attacks
articles.summary: Russia says UK decision to share missile blueprints with Ukraine is evidence of direct military involvement in the war.
articles.body:
Factories manufacturing drones in the United Kingdom for export to Ukraine could come under attack from “unknown sources”, a Kremlin adviser has said, after Britain agreed to share long-range missile blueprints with Kyiv.

Andrei Fedorov, an adviser to the Kremlin and a former deputy foreign minister, told British broadcaster BBC on Tuesday that he could not “exclude 100 percent” that there might be some “semi-military” action against Britain, as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited Ukraine.

The UK shared missile blueprints with Ukraine for it to manufacture French-British designed long-missile drones during Burnham’s first overseas trip to Kyiv on Monday. Sharing these blueprints, according to the Russian adviser, is seen by Moscow as proof of the UK’s “direct military involvement” in the Russia-Ukraine war.

Fedorov said that “sooner or later, there might be not only verbal but maybe some visible reaction from Russia towards the UK”.

Asked to elaborate, he said: “There are different discussions how it should look like – it might be so-called technical reaction, maybe some hackers attack from unknown source, not from official level, of course.”

“There might be different political steps, and I cannot exclude 100 percent that there might be some semi-military.”

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov shared similar sentiments with reporters on Monday, stating that the UK is “participating in this war” by its missile support and that this is adding “fuel to the fire”.

Burnham responded in Kyiv by asking reporters who started the fire in the first place. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The UK has agreed to declassify blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French-produced version of the Storm Shadow that has already been used to hit targets in Russia.

The Scalp missile can hit targets that are heavily fortified, such as bunkers, unlike existing Ukrainian missiles. It has a range of about 240km (149 miles).

articles.title: In 1997, a horse jumped a fence and joined one of Franceâs prestigious cycling races; it ran through the peloton and reached the front before leaving 20 kilometres from the finish
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In March 1997, amidst the professional cyclists of the Critérium International, a horse jumped onto the course, raced with the peloton, and became an unforgettable and chaotic part of the race's history.
articles.body: In March 1997, the Critérium International peloton suddenly gained an unexpected companion: a horse. The animal had jumped a fence beside the course and landed directly in the path of the fast-moving cyclists. Rather than turning away, it ran alongside the riders, moved through the group and eventually reached the front. The interruption became one of the most memorable moments in the history of the race.According to Cyclingnews, the incident took place on March 29, 1997, during the opening stage of the Critérium International, a French stage race held in the Tarn region that year. The 188-kilometre stage ran from Blaye-les-Mines to Rabastens and featured riders such as Laurent Jalabert, Marco Pantani and Chris Boardman. Late in the race, a horse escaped from a field and joined the peloton, creating confusion among the riders. The animal remained with the group for several kilometres before falling away and disappearing from the race, with reports placing the incident roughly 15 to 20 kilometres from the finish.When the peloton met a runaway horseThe riders were travelling together when the horse suddenly cleared a fence bordering the road. Television footage captured the animal landing on the course and immediately joining the stream of cyclists. For the riders, the appearance was more than a curiosity; it was a serious hazard. A horse running at speed in the middle of a tightly packed peloton could easily have caused a serious crash. Frédéric Moncassin later recalled the dramatic sound of the animal landing, describing the noise of its hooves, the sparks and its breathing. The horse, however, did not panic. It continued forward with the cyclists.Rather than remaining behind the pack, the animal began moving through it. It passed riders and worked its way towards the front, creating an extraordinary scene in which a four-legged intruder appeared to be competing against some of Europe's best professional cyclists. The horse eventually reached the front of the group and crossed the bridge at Lisle-sur-Tarn ahead of the riders. When the cyclists approached a junction, the race turned while the horse continued straight ahead, finally leaving the course and ending its unexpected appearance in the race.The race continued without its unexpected challengerThe horse may have been the most memorable part of the opening stage, but the race continued and produced a very different story over the following two stages. In the first stage, Stéphane Barthe of Casino won the 188-kilometre route from Blaye-les-Mines to Rabastens in a sprint, finishing ahead of Mario Traversoni and Frédéric Moncassin. His victory gave him the early overall lead, while the horse that had briefly joined the peloton became an unusual footnote to the day's racing.The Cyclenews also notes that the following morning overall standings changed during the mountain stage to Pic de Nore. Marcelino García of ONCE attacked on the final climb of the 80-kilometre stage and finished about a minute ahead of Laurent Jalabert and the other leading riders. The result put García into the overall lead. The race then concluded that afternoon with an eight-kilometre individual time trial in Castres. García did not need to win the stage to secure the title. His ONCE teammate Aitor Garmendia recorded the fastest time, ahead of Chris Boardman, while García finished sixth and protected his lead. He went on to win the 1997 Critérium International overall, leaving the horse as the unlikely star of the race's opening day.From cycling footage to film historyWhat began as a bizarre moment during a professional cycling race did not remain confined to the world of sport. Footage of the horse running alongside the peloton was later used in Amélie, the 2001 French film directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, giving the incident a second life on screen. The horse had appeared during the opening stage of the 1997 Critérium International, a long-running French stage race that attracted many of the sport's leading riders and was often part of their preparation for bigger races later in the season.What made the footage so striking was not simply that a horse had wandered onto the course. The animal moved alongside the peloton for several kilometres, keeping pace with the riders as they continued the stage. For a brief stretch, the professional race took on an unusual appearance, with the cyclists following their race tactics while an unexpected horse travelled among them.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In the early 2000s, Mark Magura bought a 272-acre Indiana farm;  after a 3-year restoration, 200.6 acres came back as wetland, prairie and forest for wildlife
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Mark Magura transformed his 272-acre Indiana farm into a thriving wildlife habitat, restoring wetlands, prairie, and forest. Learn about the permanent conservation easement ensuring protection for future generations.
articles.body: For more than a decade, much of Mark Maguraâs Indiana property was simply farmland, with about 220 acres leased to farmers growing crops. Today, the landscape includes wetlands, prairie, young forest and shallow seasonal ponds that provide wildlife habitat. The transformation took three years and ultimately put 200.6 acres under a permanent conservation easement, ensuring that the restored land will not return to conventional farming.According to the US Department of Agricultureâs Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS), Mark Magura bought the 272-acre property in Starke County, Indiana, in the early 2000s. For more than a decade, about 220 acres remained in agricultural production under lease agreements with different farmers. During this period, Magura began working with the NRCS to enrol parts of the property in conservation programmes aimed at addressing wet areas and improving wildlife habitat.From farmland to wildlife habitatThe first steps came well before the major restoration. In 2006, Magura enrolled portions of the farm in the Conservation Reserve Program to address wet areas around drainage ditches. NRCS provided technical assistance, while the Farm Service Agency helped fund the planting of cool-season grass filter strips. Further changes followed in 2009 and 2010. Hardwood trees were planted to provide habitat for the Indiana bat, while warm-season grasses were established along field borders to benefit quail and other upland birds. As wildlife began returning, Magura became increasingly interested in restoring a much larger portion of the property.NRCS notes that Magura began the process of enrolling about 200 acres in the Wetland Reserve Easement programme in 2018. The restoration took three years and converted former cropland into a mix of wetland, prairie and forest habitat. Once the work was completed, the easement covered 200.6 acres and placed the land under permanent conservation protection. Under its terms, the property could not be returned to conventional agriculture or subjected to major landscape-altering activities such as drainage or timbering. Magura retained ownership of the land, but accepted permanent restrictions on how it could be used. He could still enjoy the property for activities such as hiking, fishing and hunting, and he could sell it if he chose, but the conservation easement would remain attached to the property and bind future owners as well. In this way, the agreement protected the restored habitat beyond Magura's own ownership, ensuring that the land's conservation purpose would continue even if its ownership changed.Building wetlands from a former farmOne of the most ambitious parts of the project was the creation of 16 acres of macrotopography, a network of shallow, pond-like depressions across the restored landscape. The depressions were built with different depths and shapes so they could collect and retain water at different times of the year, creating varied wetland conditions across the site.Research published in Wetlands Ecology and Management found that restoring seasonal flooding can help revive seasonal patterns in waterbird communities and increase bird diversity. The researchers found that restored flooded meadows supported greater waterbird diversity, with the effects particularly evident during autumn and winter. The findings highlight the ecological value of wetlands that experience changing water levels rather than remaining permanently flooded.The restoration involved more than creating shallow depressions. Trees were planted throughout the property, while prairie areas were established with conservation cover. Together, these efforts created a mosaic of wetland, grassland and forest habitats, with transitional areas between them. Instead of providing wildlife with a single type of landscape, the restoration created a more varied environment with different habitats in proximity.When wildlife returnedFor Magura, the clearest sign that the restoration was working came from the sheer amount of wildlife. The property that had once been dominated by corn and soybean fields was soon home to birds, frogs and other animals. At one point, the wildlife was so abundant that the sounds around his home disrupted the quiet he had expected to enjoy. The transformation also changed the long-term future of the property. Instead of treating the land solely as an agricultural asset, Magura chose to make much of it a permanent wildlife habitat.The result is a reminder that restoring farmland does not necessarily mean returning it to a single, fixed type of landscape. On the property, wetlands, prairie and forest now coexist, each providing different conditions for wildlife. The work took years, but once the major construction was completed, nature took over much of the next stage. As Magura put it, the land was something people could steward rather than own forever. His three-year restoration was only the beginning. The trees will continue to grow, the prairie will develop, and the seasonal wetlands will keep changing with the water table, allowing the landscape to become increasingly self-sustaining over time.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Perfectly fine with my body’: Danish PM blasts plastic surgeon’s beauty advice
articles.summary: Mette Frederiksen, Denmark’s second female prime minister, is one of Europe’s longest-serving and most experienced leaders.
articles.body: COPENHAGEN, Denmark — Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen is fed up with getting unsolicited beauty advice. The 48-year-old wrote Monday on Instagram that she had just returned home from a trip to Ukraine, where she was exposed to air raid sirens in the ongoing war, only to find a message by a plastic surgeon offering to “fix that little spot on your nose.” “I’ve lost count of how many messages I’ve received over the years about my appearance,” Frederiksen wrote. “Especially that I have ugly teeth and thin hair. That I have an ugly ‘wart’ on my nose and well-meaning advice to get some Botox.” The prime minister of the Nordic country posted a screenshot of the plastic surgeon’s offer on Instagram but without identifying him. She also posted her response: “Oh no. I’m happy with my body — I really don’t need a male plastic surgeon to have an opinion about it!” Frederiksen, a Social Democrat and Denmark’s second female prime minister, is now in her third term, making her one of Europe’s longest-serving and most experienced leaders. She has led the European Union and NATO member country since mid-2019. She has pledged to maintain a firm stance against U.S. President Donald Trump’s ambitions for Greenland, the kingdom’s semiautonomous territory, and continue supporting Ukraine against Russia’s war of aggression. On Instagram, Frederiksen stressed that she does not interfere with other people’s looks and that “I’m perfectly fine with my body — as it is when you’re a woman approaching 50.” She added that “if you’re going to write to me (and you’re more than welcome to), I hope you’ll use your time to talk about something more meaningful. Not my nose.” The prime minister also said that those unsolicited beauty tips and suggestions made her feel “indignant” and that “today, I’m sending an extra loving thought to all of you who have to put up with the ‘perfect imperfections’ we all walk around with every day.”

articles.title: In 1959, Vermont bought Snake Mountain land but the seller kept timber rights; 67 years later the state plans to secure 949 acres of those rights and add 256 acres
articles.summary: US News: A conservation story that began nearly seven decades ago is entering a new chapter in Vermont. What was once a complicated split between land ownershi.
articles.body: A conservation story that began nearly seven decades ago is entering a new chapter in Vermont. What was once a complicated split between land ownership and timber rights at Snake Mountain is now set to be reunited, potentially giving wildlife, forests and outdoor enthusiasts greater protection for generations to come. According to media reports, with support from the Trust for Public Land, the Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department plans to secure the timber rights covering 949 acres of the Snake Mountain Wildlife Management Area (WMA). The state also plans to acquire an additional 256 acres in Addison and Weybridge, expanding the popular natural area by nearly 25%. It is reported that both transactions are expected to be completed by early 2027.A major expansion for Snake MountainLocated between Addison and Weybridge, Snake Mountain WMA currently encompasses 1,215 acres of forested landscape surrounded largely by farmland. Its proximity to some of Vermontâs largest population centres makes it an especially valuable place for people seeking access to nature. The planned 256-acre addition would expand the protected area while improving habitat connectivity. The project is also expected to create new opportunities for hiking, hunting and wildlife watching. The effort will simultaneously reunite the stateâs ownership of the land with the timber rights covering much of the WMA, allowing Vermont Fish & Wildlife to take a more coordinated approach to managing the landscape.Why timber rights matterWhen Vermont purchased the lands that became Snake Mountain WMA in 1959, the seller retained the timber rights. This meant that while the state owned the land for conservation and public access, responsibility for growing, managing and harvesting timber remained with the private owner. Such arrangements have historically been relatively common on Vermont Fish & Wildlife properties. More than six decades later, the state is seeking to bring those interests together. Acquiring the timber rights would allow Vermont Fish & Wildlife to coordinate forestry decisions with its broader goals for wildlife, recreation, water quality and habitat protection. Any future roads or skid trails required for timber harvesting could also be planned alongside conservation priorities.A haven for wildlifeSnake Mountain is far more than a scenic hiking destination. The WMA contains eight types of wetlands, including a glacial bog estimated to be about 9,500 years old. Its forests and wetlands provide habitat for a remarkable range of species. Peregrine falcons nest on the mountainâs western cliffs, while mature trees provide roosting habitat for federally endangered Indiana bats and northern long-eared bats. The landscape also supports woodland mammals, game birds, songbirds, amphibians and other wildlife. Protecting and connecting these habitats could become increasingly important as environmental conditions change.Building climate resilienceConservation groups say the expanded and reunified property could play an important role in climate resilience. The larger protected landscape would provide additional lowland forest habitat while helping safeguard wetlands and headwater streams. These interconnected natural areas can serve as important refuges for biodiversity and help species adapt as the climate changes. For a forested landscape surrounded by farmland, strengthening those connections could be particularly valuable.How the project is being fundedThe timber rights and additional acreage are being purchased from The A. Johnson Co., LLC, with funding assembled from local, state, federal and private sources. The project includes a $1.35 million grant from the US Fish & Wildlife Serviceâs Recovery Land Acquisition Grant programme, funded through the Land and Water Conservation Fund. It also includes $417,500 from the Vermont Housing & Conservation Board, support from the Town of Weybridge Conservation Fund and significant private donations. The availability of federal funding is linked largely to the habitat provided by Snake Mountain for endangered bat species.A long history of conservationThe A. Johnson Co. has managed the timber rights at Snake Mountain for decades. The company has maintained that responsible forestry can coexist with wildlife habitat, recreation and healthy natural communities. The planned transfer marks an opportunity to bring those long-standing conservation and forestry interests under unified management. Vermont Fish & Wildlife officials say the agency is particularly appreciative of the stewardship that helped maintain the quality of the landscape over the past several decades.More land could soon join the WMASnake Mountainâs expansion may not end with the 256-acre acquisition. In 2026, the WMA is also expected to receive a donation from The Nature Conservancy consisting of two adjoining parcels totalling 88 acres in Addison. Known as the Willmarth Woods Natural Area, the property contains one of the Champlain Valleyâs largest low-elevation mature forest stands. The area features rich soils supporting a high-quality mesic red oak and northern hardwood forest. It also contains the trailhead for one of the main hiking routes leading to Snake Mountainâs summit. Planned as an addition to Snake Mountain WMA since 1992, Willmarth Woods could further strengthen the ecological and recreational value of the protected landscape.Image Courtesy: istockCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Overnight raid near Haiti capital kills around 50 - here is what happened
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At least 47 people were killed and another 22 injured in an overnight attack by armed gangs in Kenscoff, a hillside community overlooking Haiti's capi.
articles.body: At least 47 people were killed and another 22 injured in an overnight attack by armed gangs in Kenscoff, a hillside community overlooking Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince. The UN estimated that casualty figures could potentially riseKenscoff, which overlooks key routes into the capital, has faced about a dozen attacks by armed gangs since last year, forcing thousands of residents to leave their homes.The gangs, operating under a broad alliance, have strengthened their control over Port-au-Prince for years and expanded into surrounding areas despite efforts by foreign countries to support Haiti's outgunned police.Haitian rights group RNDDH estimated that between 30 and 40 people were killed and 15 to 20 wounded in the latest raid. It said the attack began at around 10:30 p.m. local time and that the full death toll remained difficult to establish.The Haitian government condemned the incident as a "heinous attack" and pledged to strengthen security. However, residents called for the local police chief to resign, accusing officers of failing to protect people who were killed only minutes away from the police station."Kenscoff will not be abandoned," the Prime Minister's office said on social media, adding that government authority would be restored "without weakness and without delay."Residents forced to flee KenscoffUN estimates show that attacks in Kenscoff over two months in early 2025 killed more than 260 people and resulted in the destruction or burning of 200 homes. Around 3,000 people were forced to flee.Nearly a dozen further attacks have occurred since then, involving rape, kidnapping, arson and livestock theft.Residents said several dozen police officers attempted to repel the armed attackers during the night, with some officers reportedly injured. They also said they had not identified any gang members among those killed, Reuters reported.Local media reported that several houses were set ablaze, including the home of Jean William Pape, a prominent public health expert.Kenscoff overlooks routes leading to Petion-Ville, where several embassies, upscale hotels and the temporary seat of government are located. It also overlooks a major road connecting the capital with southern Haiti.According to Reuters, the latest violence could further raise concerns about Haiti's ability to hold an election in December, which would be the country's first in a decade. articles.title: Trump’s tariff war with Canada threatens GOP candidates in border battlegrounds
articles.summary: President Trump’s tariff war with Canada is putting vulnerable GOP candidates in border states in a precarious position about 10 weeks out from the midterms, with economic anxiety already running high. Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports took effect on Saturday after bilateral negotiations collapsed at the eleventh hour. Trump…
articles.body:
President Trump’s tariff war with Canada is putting vulnerable GOP candidates in border states in a precarious position about 10 weeks out from the midterms, with economic anxiety already running high.

Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports took effect on Saturday after bilateral negotiations collapsed at the eleventh hour. Trump threatened 50 percent tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts and steel on Monday to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Some strategists say the impact on Americans, particularly in states with close economic ties to Canada, will only compound GOP challenges around affordability, with voters losing trust in Republicans to handle the economy.

“This escalation and the timing of it are problematic,” Jason Cabel Roe, a Michigan-based Republican strategist, told The Hill.

“It really undermines our messaging when we’re trying to address affordability and we’re already having to deal with the price of oil due to the war in Iran. But that affordability debate only gets more complicated when we’re in a trade war with our largest trading partner, who happens to share a border with us,” he said.

Roe said the trade war could also be “an opportunity for Republicans to separate themselves from the president’s policy.”

The only GOP candidate to attempt to create that distance so far has been Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who is facing a tough reelection race against Democrat Troy Jackson. She has consistently spoken out against Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods, joining three other Republicans who voted with Democrats last year to undo tariffs on Canada.

This time around, she called the escalating tariffs a “mistake” and urged officials to get back to the negotiating table.

“The on-again/off-again trade talks between the U.S. and Canada lead to higher costs, risk, and uncertainty for Maine businesses. If the Administration proceeds with these tariffs, they will increase costs for Maine families, as most businesses will have no choice but to pass on the tariffs to their customers through higher prices,” she wrote on the social platform X over the weekend.

The trade war also stands to become an issue in Ohio, where Sen. Jon Husted (R) is facing a challenge from former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), and in Michigan’s open Senate race between former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and Abdul El-Sayed (D). Democrats are also seeking to zero in on the issue in Iowa and Alaska, where they see opportunities to further expand the Senate map.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has rated all four races as toss-ups.

Wayne Winegarden, senior fellow in business and economics at the Pacific Research Institute, said the tariffs would make production more costly for U.S. businesses along the border, which would adjust in ways that ultimately hurt consumers and families in those states.

Vice President Vance defended the tariffs while rallying Republicans in Maine on Monday — an event that Collins skipped. He argued the administration was seeking to protect Mainers.

“I think that we need to send a message loud and clear to the prime minister of Canada: Stop taking advantage of the people of Maine. Stop taking advantage of America. It’s over, we expect fairness in our trade policy,” Vance said.

But Democrats see political opportunity in the coming repercussions of the tariff tit for tat.

“Americans are paying more for everything because GOP Senate candidates have served as a rubber stamp for Trump’s chaotic tariffs at the expense of their states. Come November, voters will hold them accountable for making life more expensive,” said Tommy Garcia, a spokesperson for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee.

Adrian Hemond, a Michigan-based Democratic strategist, said Ohio and especially Michigan rely on trade with Canada more than other states.

“The president’s ego may have disastrous effects for Republicans politically, but there’s no question that the economic results for Michigan and Ohio will be disastrous,” Hemond said.

Rep. Chris Pappas, the Democratic Senate candidate in New Hampshire, is using the trade war to lash out at his Trump-backed Republican opponent, former Sen. John Sununu (N.H.).

“Trump creates a mess he can’t clean up. Once again,” Pappas wrote on social media on Saturday. “John Sununu won’t speak out against it. Once again.”

“Working families are paying for this recklessness,” he added.

The Cook Political Report has classified New Hampshire’s race as “lean Democratic.”

One Republican operative told The Hill that “every candidate has to run the race that they see fit.”

“They have to break with the administration when they see fit, when it benefits the state, and their region,” they said.

Canada rejected the U.S.’s terms for a trade deal late Friday, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying last-minute additions by the U.S. were “unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”

Carney said Canada would “match those tariffs dollar for dollar” starting Sept. 8 and that “additional measures” would be taken to support workers and business owners in Canada.

The collapsed deal came after weeks of intense negotiations between the U.S. and Canada.

Canada is the U.S.’s second-largest trading partner. The 50 percent tariffs that took effect this weekend impact everything from wine to hockey sticks to cement.

“Those costs are at some point going to get passed down to their consumers,” said Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute. “I don’t think something like inflation will pick up from these tariffs, but I think there’s going to be cost increases in specific sectors.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford told The Associated Press on Monday that Canada is “all in,” and he warned Republican states would face the brunt of the country’s retaliation.

“The red states we’re going to hit hard,” Ford told reporters Monday.

White House spokesperson Kush Desai defended the tariffs, saying, “President Trump ascended to the White House on a clear promise to the forgotten men and women of America that they would be forgotten no longer.”

“Countless American workers, farmers, and businesses have borne the brunt of America’s lopsided trade relations, including with Canada which has demanded total access to the American market without reciprocity. President Trump will never stop fighting to put Americans and America First,” he said.

articles.title: OnlyFans owner was paid over $700m before his death
articles.summary: The site hosts a range of subscription-based content from cooking to fitness videos, but it is best known for pornography.
articles.body:
The late owner of streaming platform OnlyFans was paid more than $700m (£513m) in dividends before his death from cancer earlier this year.

Fenix International Ltd, the British company that owns OnlyFans, made $714m in profit before tax last year, it said in its annual report. This is an increase of 5% from 2024.

The site hosts a range of subscription-based content from cooking to fitness videos, but it is best known for pornography and is credited with transforming online adult content by encouraging personal connection between sex workers and subscribers.

Its owner Leonid Radvinsky, who died earlier this year aged 43 , bought the site from its British founders in 2018.

OnlyFans employs just 47 people. Companies with such high profits rarely have such small staff - for example, British retail giant Marks and Spencer, which employs over 65,000 people, made £671m in profit last year.

Fenix International's company results show that it paid dividends of $535m for the year ending 30 November 2025, with further dividends payments totalling $174m between then and 26 March 2026.

Radvinsky, who was born in Ukraine and raised in the US, died on 23 March. The company is now owned by his widow, Yekaterina 'Katie' Chudnovsky.

OnlyFans surged in popularity during the Covid-19 pandemic, landing Radvinsky on Forbes' annual list of billionaires just three years later.

The site is known for the way it encourages creators and fans to connect through livestreams, personalised messages, and direct requests for custom-made photos and videos.

In return for hosting the material, OnlyFans takes a 20% share of all payments.

The site had 132 million paying subscribers and 2.5 million active creators in 2025.

The boom in size and popularity under Radvinsky's ownership also brought scrutiny from lawmakers and regulators over its adult content — a recent BBC Three documentary uncovered allegations of exploitation, coercion and violence committed against OnlyFans creators.

In 2024, British regulators launched an investigation into whether children were accessing porn , an issue that the company at the time blamed on a technical issue.

Ofcom ultimately dropped that probe, but it fined the firm about £1m for failing to respond accurately to its requests for information about the measures it had in place to check the age of its users, who in theory must be 18 or over.

Creators have also debunked the narrative that making explicit videos on the site is a get-rich-quick scheme.

Keily Blair, the chief executive of OnlyFans, said on Tuesday that the company had paid over $30bn to creators since launching a decade ago.

"OnlyFans provides real opportunities to real people by creating a safe, regulated space where people can monetise their content with a global fan base," she said.

articles.title: Colombian drug gangs recruiting children through social media to pilot explosive drones: Report
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Colombian drug gangs and rebel groups are increasingly recruiting children and training them for dangerous roles, including piloting drones loaded wit.
articles.body: Colombian drug gangs and rebel groups are increasingly recruiting children and training them for dangerous roles, including piloting drones loaded with explosives, Human Rights Watch said in a report published Monday.The rights watchdog said armed groups were using social media to lure children as they expanded their control over rural areas where they profit from drug trafficking, extortion and illegal mining.âArmed groups in Colombia are recruiting children with impunity,â Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch told news agency AP, warning that weak protection systems and social media platforms were making recruitment easier.Child recruitment is rising againAt least 1,500 children have been recruited by armed groups in Colombia since 2021, according to the countryâs Human Rights Defendersâ Office. Of those cases, 625 were reported in 2024 alone.Child recruitment had declined after Colombiaâs 2016 peace agreement with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, helped reduce violence in several parts of the country. But recruitment has risen again as smaller rebel factions and criminal organisations have fought to seize control of rural territories abandoned by FARC fighters.Armed groups have historically used children as messengers, cooks and intelligence gatherers, and sometimes forced them to engage with rival groups. Girls have also faced sexual abuse by commanders.But HRW said the role of recruited children was changing as armed groups increasingly turned to drones equipped with explosives. The drones have been used to attack rival groups as well as police and military bases.HRW said it had verified social media videos showing children operating explosive-laden drones and had interviewed family protection officers who work with children who escaped or were demobilised from armed groups.Some children who later left the groups said commanders had presented operating drones as a game rather than as participation in armed combat, the report said.The scale of drone attacks has also grown. Colombiaâs Human Rights Defendersâ Office recorded 121 drone attacks by armed groups in the first five months of this year, killing 21 people and injuring 145.Social media becomes a recruitment toolHRW identified dozens of social media accounts that portrayed life with rebel groups in a positive light, an issue that the United Nations has also previously raised.The watchdog said algorithms on platforms including Meta and TikTok appeared in some cases to promote content that encouraged children to join armed groups.Meta and TikTok told HRW that their platforms prohibit content promoting violence and said they had removed accounts flagged by the organisation.The FARC dissident faction led by commander Ivan Mordisco was involved in most of the child-recruitment cases identified by HRW, with particularly heavy recruitment reported in Colombiaâs Cauca region.The impact has been especially severe on Indigenous communities. Nearly half of the child-recruitment cases recorded by Colombian authorities since 2021 involved Indigenous children, even though Indigenous people account for only about 4% of the countryâs population. Girls represented 40% of all recruited children.HRW urged the Colombian government to devote more resources to prosecuting those who recruit children and strengthen protection systems in vulnerable rural areas. It also called on social media companies to make it easier for users to report recruitment content and preserve evidence that could help prosecutors.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
