articles.title: Can Pakistan’s Asim Munir convince Iran military chiefs to return to talks?
articles.summary: Pakistan says progress was made in Tehran, but Iran’s security establishment remains wary of Washington.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan — Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir spent Monday moving through the power corridors of Tehran: the presidency, parliament, the Supreme National Security Council, and the foreign and interior ministries.

He met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, as well as Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is Tehran’s chief negotiator in talks with the United States to end their now six-month-long war.

list 1 of 4 Pakistan’s army chief back in Iran: Can he break peace talks deadlock?

list 2 of 4 US launches ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ to cut Iran’s economic lifeline

list 3 of 4 Yemen’s Houthis report attack on Saudi ship

list 4 of 4 How US sanctions on Iran ripple through global markets and consumers

But amid a deadlock in those peace negotiations, many analysts say that Munir’s true test as mediator will lie in his ability to use his position as an influential military leader to convince his Iranian counterparts in olive uniforms to agree to a return to talks with Washington.

Days before Munir’s visit, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told a gathering of doctors in Tehran that it was time to end the war while Iran held the advantage, a message aimed as much at Tehran’s own security establishment as at Washington.

“It is better that we bring the war to an end now as we are in a position of power and dignity,” he said, adding that “the whole world acknowledges our victory”.

Hours later, on August 21, the chief of the general staff of Iran’s armed forces, Major-General Ali Abdollahi, promised “revolutionary, crushing, regret-inducing and devastating” responses to any American miscalculation.

It was a sharp illustration of the gap between Iran’s president and the men now running its military — one that Munir will need to also navigate, analysts say.

And that’s why Munir’s most significant meeting on Monday might have been with General Mohsen Rezaei, a representative of Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and the newly appointed secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. Rezaei is essentially the bridge between the military and Khamenei.

Munir’s visit to Tehran came on a day when the region and the world were bracing for US President Donald Trump’s threatened “economic D-Day” sanctions against Iran, accompanied by a threatened punishment for all countries that continue to trade with Tehran.

Later in the day, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled “ Operation Economic Outcast “, a sweeping sanctions campaign targeting Iran’s digital assets, gold, aviation, technology and shipping networks.

But while warning other countries to sever trade ties with Iran, he held back from actually announcing any penalties for those nations, acknowledging that such a step would “blow up the global financial system”.

Meanwhile, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaking the same day, kept the option of renewed strikes open.

“If we need to use kinetic strikes, we’ll use them. If Iran is foolish enough to overplay their hand or mess with the American military, we’ll do what we need to do,” he said.

It’s unclear whether Munir’s visit helped stave off broader US action against Iran and its trading partners.

But the timing was significant, analysts point out. Munir travelled to Tehran days after taking a phone call from United States President Donald Trump, who reportedly asked Islamabad to use its influence to bring Iran back to the table.

Pakistan’s Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said the one-day visit had produced “comprehensive discussions” on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and ending the war.

Iranian officials, the ISPR added, “appreciated Pakistan’s constructive role and sincere efforts”.

Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who travelled with Munir, went further, calling the talks “very positive and productive” and saying “significant progress was made”.

This was his fourth visit to Tehran this year, but his first since Iran’s military hierarchy changed earlier this month.

On August 10, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei installed Abdollahi as chief of the general staff and moved Rezaei into the Supreme National Security Council. Ahmad Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), has held his post since March, when his predecessor was killed in the war’s opening strikes .

It is these military men that analysts say are now shaping Iran’s war moves, potentially giving a fellow man in uniform an edge over traditional diplomats in convincing Tehran to get back to talks.

“It is increasingly the IRGC and the wider security establishment driving decisions on war and peace during this crisis,” Ahmed Saeed, a former vice admiral in Pakistan’s navy and a defence analyst, told Al Jazeera.

Naqvi, the interior minister, has travelled to Tehran eight times since April without those visits producing a substantial breakthrough.

But unlike him, Munir is not a politician. He’s a general who appears to enjoy the trust of both the Iranian leadership and, crucially, Trump — who has described the Pakistani army chief as his “favourite field marshal”.

“The call [to Munir a few days ago] was initiated by Trump himself, requesting Pakistani leadership use its influence to bring Iran back to the table,” Saeed said.

What Iranian officials actually told Munir, in accounts carried by Iranian state media, differed little from what they have been telling their own broadcasters all week.

“We distrust America, and it must change its behaviour,” Rezaei told Munir, according to IRNA.

Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker, was blunter.

“We are pursuing the implementation of the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding, and it is America that must adhere to its commitments based on the Memorandum of Understanding,” he told Munir, according to IRNA.

Pezeshkian, meanwhile, pressed Munir to tell Washington to “correct its tone and approach”, warning that “relying on force and bullying will only complicate the process”, according to Tasnim, another Iranian outlet.

Oman’s Foreign Minister Badr bin Hamad Albusaidi is also expected in Tehran today for a separate round of talks focused specifically on the Strait of Hormuz , a track that has run alongside Pakistan’s mediation for months.

Oman’s involvement is not new. Albusaidi has held recurring talks with Tehran on the strait’s navigation rules .

Ejaz Haider, a Lahore-based defence analyst, said the Omani and Pakistani diplomatic tracks complement each other.

“Oman and Islamabad channels complement, because clause 5 of the Islamabad MoU stresses a bilateral understanding on the strait [between Oman and Iran],” he told Al Jazeera. The Strait of Hormuz passes through the territorial waters of Iran and Oman.

“This [a deal between Iran and Oman to jointly manage the strait] is not in the interest of the US, which is why Trump has threatened to bomb Oman,” Haider said, referring to remarks Trump made on August 17 , when he told Fox News he would bomb Oman if it “gets in the way” of reopening the strait, the second time he had threatened the US ally over Hormuz.

Where Islamabad’s advantage as a mediator lay was in its “direct access to Vahidi, Abdollahi and Rezaei, the actual architects of Iran’s decision-making”, Saeed, the former naval official, said.

An Iranian official close to the negotiations, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Albusaidi would be in Tehran “primarily to hear what Iran has decided and what it has discussed with its Pakistani mediator”.

Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of defence studies at King’s College London, said the differences that had emerged between the Iranian military and civilian leaderships demonstrate a gulf between their understanding of where the war stood.

Pezeshkian and Ghalibaf, Krieg said, were “essentially warning that Iran cannot live indefinitely in this condition”, while “parts of the IRGC believe the opposite and think time is working against Washington”.

But ultimately, he said, “Mohsen Rezaei, Ahmad Vahidi and the IRGC are central to whether any political understanding [to end the war] can be implemented”, referring to Iran’s top military leadership.

“[Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas] Araghchi can negotiate something, and Qatar can broker it, but none of that matters if the security apparatus does not accept the operational consequences.”

For now, Munir appears to be the candidate mediators believe has the best shot at getting Iranian generals from their war room to the board room.

articles.title: Vande Mataram row: Is Congress taking a calculated gamble or walking into BJP's trap?
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Is the Congress trying to send out a subtle message signalling âsoft minority appeasementâ? Or has the party played to BJPâs strength by la.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Is the Congress trying to send out a subtle message signalling âsoft minority appeasementâ? Or has the party played to BJPâs strength by lapping up a controversy that may push it into a corner?The Congress's decision to sing only two stanzas of Vande Mataram at party events signalled a rare hardening of stance on an issue that the party knows could make it vulnerable to attacks over both minority appeasement and nationalism.As expected, the Congress decision, which cited a 1937 resolution, triggered sharp reactions from the BJP, with Union home minister Amit Shah accusing the Congress of repeating "politics of appeasement."Union minister JP Nadda also slammed the Congress, alleging that the party's 1937 resolution was driven by "appeasement politics" and contributed to the circumstances that led to the Partition. In a post on X, Nadda said the Congress' decision in 1937 to divide 'Vande Mataram' into two parts fuelled the two-nation theory and ultimately led to the partition of the country.'This was followed by attacks questioning Congressâs commitment to nationalism and patriotism.Union minister Giriraj Singh accused the Congress leadership of disrespecting the legacy of India's freedom fighters and operating under ideological pressure. "This is not just opposition to Vande Mataram but against our revolutionaries," Singh said, adding, "Now, the Congress has become the Muslim League. This is not Gandhi ji's Congress but Sonia Gandhi and Rahul Gandhi's Congress," the BJP leader said.BJP MP Dinesh Sharma also accused the opposition leadership of harbouring "Muslim League-like thinking." He equated senior Congress leaders with Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan who spearheaded the Two-Nation Theory, to criticise the Congress party's approach toward national symbols.Later, the BJP passed a resolution condemning the Congress Working Committee's decision to sing only the first two stanzas of 'Vande Mataram' and announced a nationwide campaign to raise awareness about the history and significance of the National Song.No surprises here. All these attacks were on expected lines. Surely, the Congress would have anticipated these high-pitched narratives questioning its nationalism and accusing it of appeasement.Congress fights backCongress leaders defended the party's stand, saying 'Vande Mataram' was associated with the freedom struggle and held emotional significance for the Congress. They accused the BJP of politicising the issue and diverting attention from the issue of Ram Mandir donation theft."BJP was not a part of the freedom struggle. Vande Mataram was a part of the freedom struggle; it is emotional for us, but political for them (BJP)," Venugopal said, adding, "We have been reciting Vande Mataram since 1937, more than 90 years. What is new for us?"The Congress leaders alleged that political rivals led by the BJP were deliberately stoking nationalist narratives to cover up their failures. What the Congress perhaps did not realise, or chose to ignore, was that the BJP had already set the stage for bringing Vande Mataram to the centrestage of its politics.Why the 1937 reference created more problems than it solvedBankim Chandra Chatterjee wrote âBande Mataramâ in the late 19th century in Sanskritised Bengali. The original version consisted of six stanzas. The song was first inserted into the pages of his novel, Anandamath, set during the late 18th century when famine and rebellion tore through Bengal.In 1950, alongside âJana Gana Manaâ as the national anthem, Vande Mataram received the honour of a national song following a decision of the Constituent Assembly, under the guidance of Rajendra Prasad, considering the historic role it played in Indiaâs freedom struggle.However, only the first two stanzas of the song were adopted as the national song.The Congress Working Committee (CWC), in a resolution of October 29, 1937, decided that only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram would be sung at national and public gatherings.This had followed advice from Rabindranath Tagore, who was the first to set Vande Mataram to music and publicly sing it at the 1896 Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress. In a letter to Jawaharlal Nehru, he suggested that only the first two stanzas of the song be used for public and national gatherings.Tagore then noted that the later verses â which invoked Hindu deities like Durga within the context of Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's novel Anandamathâcould alienate non-Hindu communities.The fact that the Muslim League and M A Jinnah were among the most vociferous critics of the song made the Congressâs 1937 resolution vulnerable to Muslim appeasement attacks ever since.BJPâs Vande Mataram push BJPâs Vande Mataram push began in May this year when the Union Cabinet approved a proposal to amend the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act and put the National Song, Vande Mataram, composed by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, on the same footing as the National Anthem, Jana Gana Mana.It was during the special discussion of Parliament on â150th Year of Vande Mataramâ in December last year that defence minister Rajnath Singh had strongly advocated for elevating the status of Vande Mataram to match the National Anthem. Rajnath had then accused the Congress of historically communalising the song and sidelining it due to appeasement politics.Earlier in January this year the Union home ministry had outlined appropriate conduct and protocols concerning Vande Mataram. The ministry had issued an order that all six stanzas of the official version must be rendered first whenever the National Song and the National Anthem are performed together. It said that the full six-stanza version was to be sung or played on key state occasions.These proposals became law in the just-concluded Monsoon session after Parliament amended the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, giving Vande Mataram equal legal standing to the National Anthem. The government is also midway through a year-long commemoration of Vande Mataram's 150th anniversary.The amended Act mandates Vande Mataram shall be honoured equally with âJana-Gana-Manaâ and shall have equal status with it, and whoever intentionally prevents the singing of the Indian National Anthem or causes disturbance to any assembly engaged in such singing shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or both.Could Congress have avoided this rowClearly, given the BJP moves, the Congress would have been aware of the political fallout of its Vande Mataram decision. Minority appeasement has been one of the biggest weapons, which the BJP has used very effectively to attack and corner the Congress.In the last 12 years, we have seen the Congress suffer politically over allegations of minority appeasement. The Congress leadership has tried to fight back with a calculated push for soft Hindutva. Rahul Gandhi and other top Congress leaders have visited temples to counter BJPâs attacks on minority appeasement.In the 1980s, the Congress faced a Shah Bano moment, which is still used to target and corner the party over allegations of minority appeasement. The then Congress government led by Rajiv Gandhi enacted a law in Parliament to limit a Muslim husband's maintenance obligation to the three-month iddat period, neutralizing a Supreme Court maintenance order under Section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC).Minorities, especially Muslims, for a very long time were part of Congressâs core vote bank and supported the party electorally. However, as the Congress lost political heft, the minorities gradually shifted to other regional parties. The same happened with other social groups like the SCs, STs and the OBCs. For the last many years, the Congress has been forced to align with the regional parties that weaned away its core voters. Now, as it tries to script its revival, it is trying to win back these communities into the party fold.We have seen Rahul Gandhi aggressively woo the SCs, STs and the OBCs by repeatedly taking up issues that impact them. The Congress leaderâs sustained pitch for caste census was an open move to reach out to these core voters. But when it comes to wooing back the minority voters, the Congress perhaps wants to play it safe. And itâs not just the Muslim appeasement attack that the Congress wants to avoid, it perhaps also does not want to antagonize its ally in Uttar Pradesh - the Samajwadi Party. Interestingly, Rahul and Akhilesh Yadav appeal to the same social support base and hence the alliance chemistry is always overshadowed by competing interests.It is in this context that one is left wondering: Has the Congress taken a calculated gamble?Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Iran used mosques to surveil, shoot at January protesters: Report
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iranian security forces used mosques across Tehran as bases to deploy personnel, monitor protesters and confront demonstrators during a deadly crackdo.
articles.body: Iranian security forces used mosques across Tehran as bases to deploy personnel, monitor protesters and confront demonstrators during a deadly crackdown in January, according to evidence obtained by Iran International.Intercepted radio communications, video footage and eyewitness accounts reviewed by Iran International point to security operations being conducted from several mosques in and around the Iranian capital on January 8 and 9, when large crowds took to the streets.The report said security personnel discussed deploying forces and equipment inside Imam Hossein Mosque, which Iran International geolocated to the intersection of Sattari Highway and Mokhbari Street in western Tehran. Witnesses described security activity around the mosque after electricity was cut in the area, while surveillance drones flew overhead.According to Iran International, witnesses said security personnel positioned outside some mosques engaged protesters before forces inside emerged to beat and arrest demonstrators. The evidence, the report said, suggests that some mosques functioned not merely as places of worship or gathering, but as operational bases from which security forces monitored and confronted protesters.One witness told Iran International that several people were positioned on the roof of a mosque near Kashani Boulevard in western Tehran on January 8.The reported crackdown came amid widespread protests in Iran, as authorities faced growing public anger and unrest. The unrest has since been overshadowed by the broader conflict involving Iran, Israel and the United States, with the country now facing intense military and economic pressure.Nearly six months into the war, Washington has shifted towards economic pressure, with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announcing new sanctions against nearly 60 Iran-linked entities and warning countries doing business with Tehran to cut financial ties or face retaliation.âWe are level-setting with every country to tell them our expectations. We know who they are. They know who they are,â Bessent said.Iran's rial has also fallen to a record low, while rising prices have added to pressure on ordinary people. Yet the economic strain has not so far translated into significant political pressure on Tehran.At the same time, Pakistan has sent a high-level delegation to Iran to encourage Washington and Tehran to return to negotiations, underscoring the continuing uncertainty surrounding the conflict.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: One key opens hundreds of cabins stocked with food across Norway, where no roads, staff or reception exist, only trust
articles.summary: Europe News: Deep in the Norwegian mountains, a hiker can reach a locked wooden cabin with no road leading to it, no receptionist and often no phone signal at all..
articles.body: Deep in the Norwegian mountains, a hiker can reach a locked wooden cabin with no road leading to it, no receptionist and often no phone signal at all. A single small metal key still opens the door. That same standard key works across hundreds of cabins run by Den Norske Turistforening, the Norwegian Trekking Association known as DNT. Once the lock turns, what follows looks less like checking into a hotel and more like temporarily taking over a shared household. Inside a self-service cabin, shelves may hold oatmeal, crispbread, pasta, canned soup, coffee and snacks, all left unattended and meant to be paid for honestly. The visitor records what they take, pays once they regain phone signal, fetches water, tends the stove, cleans up before leaving and stacks fresh firewood for whoever arrives next, a stranger they will likely never meet, trusting that the same system will be waiting for them on their next journey through Norway's remote wilderness.How 1 standard key came to open hundreds of different Norwegian cabinsAccording to DNT's own explanation of the cabin key system, the standard key unlocks hundreds of the organisation's unstaffed and self-service cabins across Norway. Members can obtain one for a small deposit and keep it while their membership remains active. The key provides access to participating cabins, although not every DNT property uses the same system. Some cabins remain unlocked, while others use a special key, code lock or booking-specific instructions. Cabins can also close temporarily or seasonally because of hunting, landowner agreements or wildlife protection, including measures intended to avoid disturbing migrating wild reindeer. DNT therefore advises hikers to check the individual cabin's listing before setting out.Why self-service and no-service cabins stock completely different suppliesAccording to DNT's guide to its cabin types, the network broadly includes staffed lodges, self-service cabins and no-service cabins, a distinction that matters more than it might first appear. Self-service cabins provide sleeping and cooking facilities alongside a stocked food pantry, with products priced individually and guests expected to record everything they take. No-service cabins generally provide bunks, blankets, cooking facilities and firewood, but no food for sale, meaning hikers need to bring their own provisions. Staffed lodges are different again, with hosts and served meals available during their operating season, so the same DNT network can take a hiker from a fully stocked pantry at one stop to an entirely self-sufficient kitchen at the next.How an offline payment system and a chore list keep the trust system workingDNT's cabin-payment system is designed around the fact that mobile coverage can disappear precisely where many of these cabins are located. According to DNT's guide to its cabin app, visitors can record their cabin stay and purchases while offline and complete payment once their phone reconnects to a network. The system therefore depends heavily on visitors honestly recording what they have used, with no cashier or attendant standing beside the pantry shelves.The same principle applies to maintaining the cabins. According to DNT's cabin-visit guide, guests are expected to handle many of the ordinary chores themselves, including fetching water, tending the wood stove, washing dishes and cleaning the spaces they use. Before leaving, visitors are asked to leave the cabin ready for the next person, including cleaning used areas and preparing firewood. The expectation is simple: the next hiker should find the cabin at least as good as the previous visitor found it.Why Norway's cabin trust system rests on far more than 1 honest hikerThe scale behind the system is considerable. According to DNT's own history, the organisation was founded in 1868 to make Norwegian nature easier and more affordable to experience. Today, its network includes more than 600 cabins spread across mountain ranges, forests, coastlines and former farmsteads throughout the country.The system works because the responsibility is distributed. Local member associations, volunteers and cabin wardens help restock food, repair buildings, maintain paths, split firewood and keep the properties functioning. Every hiker who records their purchases, cleans a room, carries water or prepares wood is therefore contributing to a much larger system that depends on thousands of small acts of cooperation. The remarkable part is not really that one key can open hundreds of doors. It is that behind each door is an unwritten agreement: take what you need, pay what you owe, clean up after yourself and leave something useful for the stranger who comes next.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Scientists planted 133 portable seismometers around Yellowstoneâs Old Faithful for two weeks; tiny ground vibrations revealed an underground hot-water reservoir holding about 79 million gallons
articles.summary: US News: Old Faithful may be the worldâs most famous geyser, but until recently, no one had a clear picture of the âplumbingâ that powers its eruptions. In a l.
articles.body: Old Faithful may be the worldâs most famous geyser, but until recently, no one had a clear picture of the âplumbingâ that powers its eruptions. In a landmark 2017 studytitled 'Anatomy of Old Faithful From Subsurface Seismic Imaging of the Yellowstone Upper Geyser Basin', University of Utah scientists deployed 133 small, portable seismometers around Old Faithful and nearby Geyser Hill for two weeks, listening to the faint hum of the ground between eruptions. By turning everyday micro-vibrations, caused by wind, water, tourists, and the geyserâs own boiling, into a usable signal, the team mapped a hidden reservouir of hot water beneath the surface. Their analysis suggests the reservoir can hold roughly 300,000 cubic meters of water, or about 79 million gallons. Based on the reportings from the University of Utah and the U.S. Geological Surveyâs Yellowstone Volcano Observatory, here's more details about the discovery:Why Old Faithfulâs underground system was a mysteryOld Faithful erupts like clockwork every 44 to 125 minutes, drawing millions of visitors to Yellowstone National Park each year. Yet despite its fame, the near-surface geology and fluid pathways feeding the geyser were poorly understood. Deep magma reservoirs 5â40 km below the park provide heat, but the shallow âplumbingâ that channels hot water to the vent had never been mapped in detail. Traditional seismic methods that rely on large earthquakes or active sources (like hammer strikes or small explosions) arenât ideal in a sensitive, crowded tourist area. The National Park Service specifically asked researchers to survey the Old Faithful area to better manage buildings and walkways constructed over thermal features that can create excessive subsurface heat.Turning noise into a map: the 133-seismometer experimentTo capture the subtle signals, the University of Utah team used compact, autonomous seismometers developed for the oil and gas industry. Each unit is a white canister about six inches high, self-contained and inexpensive compared to traditional instruments that can cost over $10,000. In 2015, researchers placed 133 of these sensors around Old Faithful and Geyser Hill for a two-week campaign, creating a dense network capable of detecting tiny ground movements.Instead of creating their own seismic source, the scientists treated ambient noise as data. They used continuous ground shaking from humans, cars, wind, water, and Yellowstoneâs hydrothermal activity, then extracted coherent signals from the background vibration. Doctoral student Sin-Mei Wu and co-author Fan-Chi Lin developed analysis methods that correlated signals from sensors near persistent hydrothermal sources to others across the array, effectively using the geyser system itself as a seismic source. This approach allowed them to image shallow structures without disturbing the fragile environment of the Upper Geyser Basin.What the tremors revealed: a giant hidden reservoirThe sensors recorded a striking pattern: bursts of intense seismic tremors around Old Faithful lasting about 60 minutes, separated by roughly 30 minutes of quiet. Counterintuitively, the eruption does not occur at the peak of shaking but at the end, just before the tremors subside. After an eruption, the geyserâs underground cavity refills with hot water. As it fills, pressurized bubbles rise, cool rapidly, and implode; the energy from these implosions generates the pre-eruption tremors.When analyzing the data, the team noticed that tremor signals from Old Faithful were not reaching the western boardwalk. Seismic waves from another hydrothermal feature to the north also slowed and scattered in nearly the same area. With the dense sensor network, they could pinpoint the shape, size, and location of the anomaly: Old Faithfulâs hydrothermal reservoir. Wu estimates the reservoirâa network of cracks and fractures through which water flows, is about 200 meters in diameter, slightly larger than the University of Utahâs Rice-Eccles Stadium, and can hold approximately 300,000 cubic meters of water, or more than 79 million gallons. By comparison, each eruption releases only around 30 cubic meters (nearly 8,000 gallons), meaning the reservoir is vastly larger than any single eruption.Why this matters for science and park managementMapping Old Faithfulâs underground system does more than satisfy curiosity. It helps park managers understand where heat and fluid flow beneath buildings, walkways, and visitor areas, informing safer infrastructure planning in one of the worldâs most visited geothermal zones. The study also demonstrates a powerful, low-impact method for imaging shallow geology in sensitive environments by leveraging ambient noise instead of active sources.For researchers, the work opens new questions about how subsurface structures change over time and how seismic waves propagate through hydrothermal systems. The team returned for additional surveys in 2016 and planned further deployments, aiming to produce even higher-resolution images and explore other basins like Norris, the parkâs hottest geothermal area. As Fan-Chi Lin noted, breakthroughs in Yellowstone depend on both new techniques and long-term relationships with the park: a reminder that some of the most iconic natural wonders still have secrets waiting beneath the surface.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 1,000 people in Japan join forces to pull a 400-ton castle keep back toward its original position after it was moved 78 meters for repairs
articles.summary: Rest of World News: About 1,000 people in Japan joined forces on Sunday to help pull the roughly 400-ton keep of Hirosaki Castle back toward its original position, more t.
articles.body: About 1,000 people in Japan joined forces on Sunday to help pull the roughly 400-ton keep of Hirosaki Castle back toward its original position, more than a decade after the historic structure was moved nearly 78 meters for repairs. Participants in Aomori Prefecture were divided into groups and used ropes to pull a cart carrying the castle keep, moving the massive structure 109 centimeters closer to its original location. The unusual public event is part of a major restoration project aimed at returning the keep to where it stood before its relocation in 2015. About 4,000 people are scheduled to participate in similar events, with the public effort expected to move the keep about 5 meters in total as the centuries-old castle begins its journey home.1,000 people pull 400-ton castle keep toward its original positionThe rope-pulling event took place at Hirosaki Castle in Aomori Prefecture, northeastern Japan, on August 23, with about 1,000 people selected by lottery taking part. Participants were divided into groups and pulled ropes attached to a cart carrying the roughly 400-ton keep. Their combined effort moved the structure 109 centimeters toward its original position. The event is part of a series of public participation activities scheduled between August 22 and 30, with about 4,000 people expected to take part. Together, the events are intended to move the keep about 5 meters, allowing members of the public to play a direct role in the highly unusual restoration project. One participant, 16-year-old high school student Mei Umetsu, said she had also helped pull the keep 11 years earlier when it was moved away from its original site.Why the castle keep was moved 78 meters in 2015The keep was moved in 2015 because the stone walls supporting Hirosaki Castle needed extensive repairs. Rather than dismantling the historic structure itself, restoration teams moved the keep away from its original foundation so workers could safely work on the aging masonry underneath it. The keep was shifted approximately 77.6 meters, or about 78 meters, from its original position. The relocation allowed specialists to dismantle and rebuild the supporting stone wall while protecting the historic wooden keep. The current project is effectively reversing that earlier move, with the keep now being returned to the location it occupied before the repairs began.How Japan repaired the castleâs historic stone wallsThe restoration of Hirosaki Castleâs stone walls was a major undertaking involving thousands of individual stones. According to Hirosaki City, workers dismantled and documented 2,185 stones before rebuilding the wall. The stones were carefully recorded so they could be returned to their appropriate positions during reconstruction, helping preserve the historic character and construction methods of the castle. The stone-wall rebuilding was completed in December 2024, clearing an important stage of the restoration project and allowing preparations for the keepâs return to move forward. Further structural and seismic work is also planned to improve the stability of the castle and protect it for the future.The 400-ton keep is slowly making its way homeThe August rope-pulling event represents only a small part of the keepâs approximately 78-meter journey back to its original position. The public events are designed to move the structure around 5 meters in total, while the remaining distance will be covered through the broader restoration operation. Officials plan to have the keep returned to its original location by the end of 2026. The spectacle of people physically pulling such a massive historic structure has attracted attention because it combines traditional methods, modern engineering and community participation. The operation is carefully planned to ensure that the centuries-old keep can be moved without damaging the historic structure.What happens to Hirosaki Castle after the moveThe return of the keep will not mark the end of the restoration project. Additional preservation and seismic reinforcement work will continue after the structure reaches its original position. The keep is one of Japanâs 12 surviving original castle keeps and is the only surviving original keep in the Tohoku region, making its preservation particularly significant. The present three-story keep dates to 1810, after an earlier castle tower was destroyed by fire. Hirosaki Castle itself was originally constructed in 1611. The keepâs interior has been closed to visitors since November 2025 and is expected to remain closed for several years while further preservation work is carried out, meaning the remarkable return journey is only one stage in the long-term effort to protect the historic castle.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: "El bótox ya le está afectando la memoria": José Manuel Figueroa cuenta su verdad ante las acusaciones de Ninel Conde
articles.summary: El cantante revive un episodio con ella y su entonces novia Angélica Vale en su casa que contradice lo contado por Ninel. "La veo tan desesperada".
articles.body:
Ya han pasado más de 20 años desde que José Manuel Figueroa y Ninel Conde acabaron su relación sentimental, pero el pleito continúa y los episodios vividos siguen saliendo a la luz. Eso sí, con versiones bien opuestas. El cantante decidió reaccionar a unas fuertes declaraciones de la artista mexicana quien, sin mencionar su nombre pero sí dándolo a entender, volvió a hacer graves acusaciones. Fue en el nuevo reality de ViX, Ninel Conde Sin Filtro , donde el Bombón Asesino compartió que, supuestamente, su expareja le había sido infiel con Angélica Vale durante su relación.

Ante los medios, Figueroa negó la versión de la actriz y aseguró que cuenta con una testigo que puede respaldar su relato: la propia Vale, quien en aquel momento era su enamorada. "El bótox ya le está haciendo mal, le está afectando la memoria, no recuerdo el episodio así", respondió José Manuel a los micrófonos que lo esperaban. El hijo de Joan Sebastián describió la escena que, confirmó, también vivió Angélica desde el otro lado del teléfono y que nada tendría que ver con la relatada por Ninel. No le fue infiel porque su pareja entonces era La Novia de México , y no ella. Insistió.

Figueroa también fue contundente al explicar por qué, en aquel momento, veía un futuro diferente con Vale. "En Ninel no veía una madre, no veía una esposa, una persona con el compromiso de casarse, y en Angélica sí, y al pasar del tiempo no me equivoqué, es una gran madre", afirmó sobre su relación con la hija de Angélica María , dejando claro que sus expectativas sentimentales eran distintas y que su historia con esta última fue realmente bonita y dulce.

El cantante se mostró todavía más duro al referirse a la situación actual de Ninel, a quien señaló de inventar historias y aprovechar el foco de los realities para siempre manchar su imagen: "La veo tan desesperada de no poder enfrentar el espejo ante la edad y aceptar su realidad, no tiene nada de malo envejecer con dignidad... La veo perdida". Sus palabras llegan mientras Conde atraviesa un momento especialmente visible de su carrera, con su participación en Top Chef VIP , además de la exposición que ha tenido a través de su reality.

Por último, Figueroa reaccionó a otra de las afirmaciones de Ninel, donde habla de violencia y actitudes machistas. "Ahora reniega de que yo la hice famosa, cuando era mi pareja luché con la disquera que no creía en ella", aseguró José Manuel, defendiendo que durante los años que fueron pareja él sí intervino para apoyarla profesionalmente y celebró sus éxitos.

Una batalla que parece no tener fin y en la que José Manuel ha asumido, según dijo a los medios, que, como siempre, nadie le iba a creer. Igualmente decidió hablar, contar su verdad y no permitió que su nombre siga manchándose.

articles.title: In 1972, Lyndon and Lady Bird Johnson gave the Texas White House and about 600 acres to the US but kept lifetime rights; she continued living there until 2007
articles.summary: US News: In 1972, former US President Lyndon B Johnson and his wife, Lady Bird Johnson, gave their ranch house and about 600 acres of land to the National Park.
articles.body: In 1972, former US President Lyndon B Johnson and his wife, Lady Bird Johnson, gave their ranch house and about 600 acres of land to the National Park Service for use as a national historic site. However, the couple retained a 'life estate', which allowed them to continue living at the property during their lifetimes.According to Seattle Times, the ranch, near Stonewall, Texas, became known as the 'Texas White House' during Johnsonâs presidency. He used the property as a retreat from Washington and hosted foreign leaders and other important visitors there. It also became a place where he held meetings and spent time away from the White House.The main house did not immediately became open to the public. The Johnsons retained the right to use the home, and after Lyndon Johnson died in January 1973, Lady Bird Johnson continued to live there under the arrangement. She remained connected to the ranch for the rest of her life.Lady Bird Johnson died in July 2007 at the age of 94. Her death ended the lifetime arrangement and allowed the National Park Service to take over the main house. By then, much of the ranch was already open to visitors.Story of the âTexas White HouseâLyndon Johnson bought the property from his aunt in 1951. During his presidency, it became closely linked to his time in office. The ranch offered Johnson a place away from Washington where he could work and meet visitors.He served barbecue to world dignitaries there and hosted several foreign heads of state. Staff meetings were also held outside, under the shade of a large oak tree.The property, however, was more than a place connected to Johnsonâs presidency. Lady Bird Johnson called it her 'heartâs home'. âIt was always Lyndonâs favorite time, particularly around sunset, from the earliest spring until cold weather drove us in,â she once said.Lady Bird Johnson also appeared to think about what would happen to the home after her family was gone. In 1965, after visiting Thomas Jeffersonâs Monticello, she spoke about looking at the Johnson house differently.âI did find myself looking at the house with new eyes, the eyes of someone who someday might leave a simple house, not anything so great in our history as Monticello, but one to which other generations of American tourists might come,â she said.Seven years later, the Johnsons made the property part of the public historical record. In December 1972, they gave the ranch house and hundreds of acres to the public as a national historic site, while retaining their life estate.Lady Bird Johnson's time at the ranchThe donation became especially significant after Lyndon Johnson died on January 22, 1973, at his LBJ Ranch. Under the terms of the life estate, Lady Bird Johnson could continue to live on and use the property, including the ranch house, for the rest of her life.She had a house in Austin, but the ranch remained important to her. A longtime family friend, Neal Spelce, said she returned to the property as often as she could. âShe would get away to the ranch as often as she could. It really was her home,â Spelce said.The ranch was already being visited by members of the public, but the main house remained off-limits while Lady Bird Johnson lived there. Visitors could take tours through the property and walk up to the family cemetery. Lady Bird was also known to sometimes wave at tour buses passing by.Spelce said the ranch had a relaxed atmosphere despite its connection to the presidency. âThere really was no pretense. It was a place where you felt you could take off your shoes and kick your feet up,â he said.Lady Bird Johnson continued to live at the ranch part-time until her death in 2007. She was buried beside Lyndon Johnson in the familyâs private cemetery, less than a mile from the ranch house.Home prepared for public toursAfter Lady Bird Johnsonâs death, the National Park Service was set to take over the 4,000-square-foot ranch house. The Johnson family was given time to remove personal belongings before officials began preparing the home for public tours.Officials considered recreating much of the interior so that it would look as it did between 1963 and 1973, when Lyndon Johnson was president. They also wanted the presentation to reflect Lady Bird Johnsonâs life at the ranch after her husbandâs death.The house itself had grown considerably over the years. Its original section was a one-room cabin with a loft built by German immigrant William âPolecatâ Meier. By 2007, it had become a 28-room building with eight bedrooms and nine bathrooms.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Ghost in PM office? When cockroaches left Japan's Sanae Takaichi screaming
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said she has not encountered any ghosts at the official residence, but recently found herself unable to kill a .
articles.body: Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said she has not encountered any ghosts at the official residence, but recently found herself unable to kill a cockroach that appeared there. She linked her hesitation to ideas about reincarnation that have stayed with her since childhood.She recounted the episode on X while answering a question she said she often receives about whether she has encountered ghosts at the residence. âIâve never encountered a ghost, but until recently, I was the one screaming when I came across cockroaches,â she wrote.âFirebirdâ shaped her responseTakaichi said she has read Osamu Tezukaâs Firebird repeatedly since childhood and that its depiction of reincarnation made a deep impression on her. The idea that âlife is connected, changing formsâ stayed with her as she grew older.She said that may be why she still cannot bring herself to kill insects, including cockroaches. When one appeared at the official residence, she recalled thinking: âMaybe this life is also part of that long cycle of reincarnation.âInstead of killing it, she left the cockroach alone for a while and hoped it would eventually make its own way out.Cockroach appeared despite precautionsHer previous accommodation, the membersâ dormitory, had never presented the same problem, she said. After moving into the official residence, she took several precautions to keep the place clean.She dealt carefully with food waste, cleaned around the dining area and washed used plastic containers. Even so, she was startled when a cockroach suddenly appeared near her feet.For some time, she kept the problem to herself and waited for the insect to leave. When she eventually told her secretaries what she had been doing, they were appalled.âOperation Combatâ ended sightingsâItâs unclean. Iâll handle it,â she quoted one of her secretaries as saying. The secretary then arranged what she called âOperation Combatâ.The measures worked, and she said there were no further cockroach sightings. Her reaction, however, was not entirely one of relief: âI felt relieved, but also a little lonely, or maybe sadâ¦â she wrote.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: China hits out at 'illegal' new US sanctions on Iran and trading partners
articles.summary: The US has threatened to isolate nations that continue to do business with Tehran, which sells much of its oil to Beijing.
articles.body:
China has vowed to protect its interests after the US announced plans to widen economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, which include Beijing.

Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said China was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.

This came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the new measures on Monday, warning any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, although the trade has declined under the US blockade of Iran's ports.

Lin said: "Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted."

Bessent described the plans for sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever" against Iran, warning banks and businesses would share in Iran's isolation if they refused to cut ties with the country.

He declined to focus on specific nations, but said US President Donald Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime".

However, responding to a question about Chinese banks, Bessent said he wanted to make clear "no one was above the reach of US sanctions".

The announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.

Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.

Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.

China's response followed Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh saying Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he said would lead to "another defeat" for the US.

"The government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he told state television.

"We also have our own tools and know how to play the game," he said, adding Tehran had been "waiting for these plans for a long time".

Iran says it is 'fully prepared' to counter widened US economic sanctions Published 16 hours ago

Iran says it is 'fully prepared' to counter widened US economic sanctions

The US has dubbed its latest sanctions "Operation Economic Outcast" and described them as an "economic D-Day" against Iran.

It comes almost six months after the start of the Iran war.

The conflict has since led to hikes in oil prices worldwide, with Tehran effectively blocking exports through the Strait of Hormuz - a waterway vital to the global economy. The US has also slowed traffic via its own naval blockade.

Recent attempts to end the conflict via diplomacy have failed, and a 60-day ceasefire formally expired last week with no sign of a settlement.

With the announcement of new sanctions, the US treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it".

UK Chancellor John Healey said the British government supported "US work to secure a diplomatic solution and welcome efforts to increase pressure".

Iran is already under heavy sanctions from the US, but Bessent said these go further.

He said the Treasury had mapped financial channels, facilitators and networks used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil, imposing sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels.

But analysts had cast doubt on the latest measures even before China's response.

David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told the BBC the direct impact on Iran's energy revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib".

"We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term," he added.

This is partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, he said, "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either".

Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group, said: "Generally, the Chinese are against unilateral sanctions. They would comply with multilateral or international sanctions, but unilateral sanctions just imposed by the US - they have always seen that as illegitimate."

And although Iran's neighbours like Pakistan, Turkey and Iraq want to maintain good relationships with the US, they "can't really afford to cut off ties with Iran", Vaez told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He said putting economic pressure on Tehran "doesn't work" because the Iranian regime is willing to "absorb any pain" and pass it onto the people.

Other trade partners that could be affected by the US announcement include India and Russia, who have not yet responded.

articles.title: India faces criticism from UN discrimination watchdog
articles.summary: CERD says India must tackle hate crimes against Bengali-speaking Muslims and increase protections for other groups.
articles.body:
A United Nations watchdog has said India must step up protections for tribal peoples and disadvantaged castes facing extrajudicial killings, torture and other violence by law enforcement.

The UN Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination (CERD) also said that the world’s most populous nation urgently needs to tackle hate crimes against Bengali-speaking Muslims.

“The committee was gravely concerned about reports of large-scale violations perpetrated by law enforcement officials against ethnic and ethno-religious groups, Indigenous and Tribal Peoples, including Scheduled Tribes, Scheduled Castes, particularly Dalits, and non-citizens,” it stated in a release on its findings on Tuesday.

“These included racially motivated violence, excessive use of force, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary and prolonged detention without due process, torture, ill-treatment and sexual violence.”

The committee urged India to investigate all such claims and bring those responsible to justice.

Caste remains a major determinant of social status in India, dictating access to resources, education and opportunity. The system, rooted in historic social hierarchical structures, separates Hindus by function and social standing.

CERD is a panel of 18 independent rights experts that monitors compliance with the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination by the 182 countries that are party to it.

Under the convention, which entered into force in 1969, countries must eliminate racial discrimination, eradicate practices of segregation and ensure equality before the law.

India appeared for review before CERD earlier this month, for the first time since 2007, with Solicitor General Tushar Mehta leading its delegation.

The committee pointed to an increase in law enforcement operations targeting Rohingya, Bengali-speaking Muslims, migrants and asylum seekers.

It said police stops and identity checks involving racial profiling had reportedly led to arbitrary arrest and detention without due process, as well as torture and mistreatment.

The committee also expressed concerns about deportations and forced returns of individuals requiring international protection.

It urged India to “urgently address discrimination, hate speech and hate crimes” against these groups, protect their rights and refrain from collective expulsions.

CERD’s opinions and recommendations are non-binding but hold significant reputational weight.

In a statement, India’s mission said that, during the review, its delegation “highlighted our pluralism; diversity; scale and complexity; constitutional and legal framework and safeguards … as we continue our journey towards ensuring equality, dignity and opportunity for all Indians”.

articles.title: Young care leavers dying early a 'national tragedy'
articles.summary: Those leaving care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review reveals.
articles.body:
Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review shows.

Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.

On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today , report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.

There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.

John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in.

"I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.

Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.

The report, co-authored by social worker Clare Chamberlain and commissioned by the Department for Education, found 18 appeared to be a significant turning point.

Of the deaths, 22 occurred at 18 – more than any other age in the range – which the review said was "strongly suggestive of the stark challenges and pressures" faced by these young people when they leave care.

Just over a third (40) of the care leavers were thought to have died by suicide, a rate the report said was potentially five times higher than that of the general population.

Other causes included murder, road traffic accidents and drug misuse, as well as potential mismanagement of medical conditions like diabetes.

The report calls for better ways to prepare young people for adulthood and an overhaul of the workforce supporting them.

The main source of support provided to young people who have left care comes through the framework of having a personal adviser (PA).

The review found that the support provided by PAs can "vary greatly from place to place" with a "huge variation" in quality of practice.

With minimum visiting requirements of once every two months, the authors say it is "not surprising" that some PAs they spoke to "hardly knew" the young person they were supporting.

The report is also critical of the housing and accommodation support given to young adults, saying it is often from a "profit-making arm of the service with no specific requirements for a therapeutic or social work discipline", which needs to be redressed.

The government says it is driving forward a national rollout of connected housing options for those leaving care, starting with £25 million this year.

It says this will "significantly increase" young people's chances of being offered a "home that provides them with community and connection rather than leaving them isolated in inappropriate accommodation".

Children's Minister Josh MacAlister said "enduring relationships" must become the "central obsession" of the care system.

"Care must build and not break the relationships that young people need, and this must be the new North Star," he added.

Izy Winter was put into care at 13. Now 25, she says she was let down at every stage.

"While I was in care I was cold, hungry and neglected," she says.

As a care leaver she experienced failures that left her feeling "invisible and unprotected".

Izy was living with an abusive partner, but welfare checks that should have picked up on this were not carried out correctly, she says.

"The person who was meant to check asked to meet me in the car park and got me to sign a piece of paper to say he'd been inside my home when he hadn't," she said.

Izy has ADHD and dyslexia and struggles with paperwork. Her support worker did not check that she was receiving all the financial support she was entitled to. By the time she was made aware, it was too late and she could not reclaim the money she had missed out on.

"I was really struggling financially and was so frustrated that even when I asked for help, I wasn't given it."

She says she is saddened, but not surprised, to read the new report.

"The recent findings reflect a reality that too many of us have lived through".

If you've been affected by the issues in this story, you can find information, advice and support from the BBC's Action Line . Anyone feeling emotionally distressed or suicidal can call Samaritans for free on 116 123 or visit samaritans.org in the UK.

articles.title: US diplomats heading back to Middle East as immediate Iran war risk recedes: Report
articles.summary: US News: The United States is preparing to return diplomats to several Middle Eastern embassies that were evacuated during the war with Iran, according to a re.
articles.body: The United States is preparing to return diplomats to several Middle Eastern embassies that were evacuated during the war with Iran, according to a report by the New York Times. The move suggests Washington does not expect a return to full-scale fighting in the immediate future.According to an internal State Department document cited by NYT, Foreign Service officers could begin returning to their posts as early as this week. The plan covers US diplomatic missions in Israel, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Oman, Iraq and Kuwait.The US Embassy in Lebanon is expected to be the first to receive returning diplomats, although it will continue operating below full staffing. Under the plan, staffing would eventually return to full strength in Israel, Jordan and Oman.Embassies in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Lebanon would initially operate at up to 85% staffing, while missions in Iraq, Kuwait and Bahrain would be capped at 75%.The State Department said it was continually reviewing security conditions at its diplomatic missions and adjusting staffing levels to allow the US to pursue its foreign-policy objectives while protecting personnel.The planned return comes despite the fact that US-Iran talks have stalled and Washington has continued to increase economic pressure on Tehran.The US announced a fresh round of sanctions on August 24 targeting Iranian military activities, procurement networks, cyber operations and petroleum trade.The decision to bring diplomats back nevertheless represents a significant shift from earlier this year. The US began reducing its diplomatic presence in the region after tensions with Iran escalated in February, with nonessential personnel and family members evacuated from several posts. Some embassies were subsequently hit or targeted by drones and rockets during the conflict.Former US officials said the redeployment could indicate that Washington believes the immediate risk of renewed fighting has fallen. But they cautioned that it should not be interpreted as proof of a lasting peace. Restrictions on family members at several Gulf missions also suggest that the State Department continues to see an elevated security threat.The move is less a declaration that the Iran conflict is over and more a signal that Washington believes its diplomats can begin returning while the fragile post-war standoff continues.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: CIA director flies unannounced to Moscow to hold talks, source says
articles.summary: CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Russia to holds talks in Moscow, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — CIA Director John Ratcliffe flew to Russia to hold unspecified talks in Moscow, according to a person with knowledge of the matter. The person declined to say whom Ratcliffe was meeting with or what the focus of the talks was. The CIA declined to comment. It’s Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Moscow as CIA director. He made headlines with a visit to Venezuela in January to meet with interim President Delcy Rodríguez about two weeks after the U.S. military seized President Nicolás Maduro in a raid in Caracas. He also traveled to Cuba in May to meet with government leaders. He was the highest-ranking Trump administration official to visit the island, which is under severe economic pressure after the U.S. tightened sanctions. News of Ratcliffe’s travel came as mystery swirled around a U.S. military transport aircraft that landed in Moscow, according to tracking data. It was not known who was on board the plane and why it was in Moscow. When asked, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he did not have information about the aircraft. Neither U.S. military officials, the White House, the U.S. Embassy in Moscow nor the Russian Embassy in Washington immediately responded to questions about the flight’s mission. Two planes, a C-130 cargo plane and a C-40, landed in Riga, the capital of Latvia, as part of the same mission, according to a U.S. official. The C-130 then went on to Russia, the official said. Data from FlightRadar24 tracking site showed a plane approached Vnukovo International Airport in Moscow just after 10 a.m. local time (3 a.m. ET) after taking off from Riga two hours earlier. It had departed from the U.S. Air Force’s Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Sunday just before 5 p.m. ET, the data showed. That plane had apparently left Moscow on Tuesday afternoon, according to flight radar data. CBS News and Axios first reported on the CIA chief’s unannounced visit. CIA directors sometimes act as envoys for presidents in high-stakes talks with adversaries. Former President Joe Biden turned to then-CIA Director William Burns to relay stern warnings to Russia before and after President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

articles.title: Rajnath approves transfer of tech of DRDO missile systems to domestic industry to reduce import dependence
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: In a big development to empower Indian private players with new missile technologies to achieve govtâs vision of self-reliance in defence p.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a big development to empower Indian private players with new missile technologies to achieve govtâs vision of self-reliance in defence production, defence minister Rajnath Singh has âapproved the transfer of DRDO-developed technologies of all conventional missile systems to the domestic industry for production within the countryâ.Conventional missiles are non-strategic, non-nuclear guided weapon systems designed and developed by DRDO for tactical and traditional battlefield operations. The initiative aims to enhance operational capability, reduce import dependence and increase domestic value addition, while supporting the growth of Indiaâs defence manufacturing sector, a defence ministry statement said on Tuesday.âThough DRDO has already tied up with several defence PSUs and private companies like L&T, Tata Advanced Systems, Bharat Forge and Adani Defence in some missile and defence system programmes, the govt is taking this big step to increase the number of production partners to ensure its supply chain for missiles and their systems are not crippled during the time of conflict in future,â a source in the defence ministry told TOI.DRDO has developed a wide array of conventional (non-strategic) missile systems spanning air defence, strike and anti-armour roles. âThe missiles that are set to become part of technology transfer include surface-to-air missile Akash (can intercept fighter jets, cruise missiles, and drones), Nag (all-weather, fire-and-forget, anti-tank guided missile), Very Short Range Air Defence System (VSHORDS counters low-altitude aerial threats at short ranges); Astra (beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile), Rudram (anti-radiation missile series designed for suppression of enemy air defences) Pralay (short-range, surface-to-surface quasi-ballistic missile) and man-portable ATGM,â the source said.The transfer of technology marks an important milestone in promoting greater participation of the domestic industries in the defence ecosystem by enabling them to undertake indigenous production, as per applicable qualifications, certifications and regulatory requirements, the ministry said.The move has come in the wake of DRDO recently inviting domestic private companies to be âpartner in the development and production of missile and bomb weapon system projects of missiles and strategic systems clusterâ.The objective of the missile tech transfer move is to enhance domestic manufacturing capabilities, strengthen defence industrial base and create opportunities for the participation of Indian MSMEs and other technology partners in the supply chain, it said.The provision will enable successful transition of missile system development to industrial production, reflecting the continued efforts of DRDO to leverage the capabilities of the Indian industry for the development and manufacture of advanced defence systems, the ministry said.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy âcriminally responsibleâ for killing her children, psychologist testifies
articles.summary: Closing arguments are expected this week in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, who killed her three young children â Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months â at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023.
articles.body:
What to know about the trial Closing arguments are expected this week in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, who killed her three young children â Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months â at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. Prosecutors say Clancy deliberately killed her kids, arguing that she sent her husband out on errands before strangling the children and then attempting suicide. The defense says Clancy was experiencing postpartum psychosis and was unable to appreciate the wrongfulness of her actions. Forensic psychologist Kirk Heilbrun is back on the stand Tuesday after he brought up Clancyâs Catholic faith, which prompted defense attorney Kevin Reddington to request a mistrial. The judge denied the motion but instructed jurors to dismiss the comments and sent them home early. Heilbrun and Reddington clashed frequently on Tuesday. Heilbrun said Clancy had "moral awareness" of what she was doing and was criminally responsible for killing her children. Reddington aggressively questioned Heilbrun's qualifications and diagnosis. The second witness called by prosecutors on Tuesday was forensic psychiatrist Dr. Gregory Saathoff. Saathoff pointed out inconsistencies in Clancy's story and said her description of the voice telling her to kill her children was not typical for these kinds of auditory hallucinations. The closely watched trial has drawn national attention, particularly around postpartum psychosis and maternal mental healthcare.
