articles.title: Could Iran’s regime collapse? Experts assess Bessent’s bid to sever financial lifelines
articles.summary: Scott Bessent's "Economic D-Day" against Iran sent the rial to an all-time low as experts debate whether maximum pressure can trigger regime change.
articles.body: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s Monday announcement that America will impose the economic equivalent of the military campaign that defeated Nazi Germany on the Islamic Republic of Iran could set off a series of events leading to the dissolution of the nearly 47-year-old dictatorship in Tehran, according to Iran experts. Bessent’s declaration of economic warfare follows President Donald Trump’s commitment last week to launch an "economic D-Day" against the Tehran regime. The comprehensive U.S. economic pressure point campaign targeting Iran’s already troubled economy could have dramatic effects on the restive population in the country of over 90 million people. "In the Second World War, D-Day marked the historic beginning of a campaign with our allies to target and drive the enemy from its positions, including those in third countries. Today, in that same spirit, we are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe," said Bessent. He added that "Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone. Iran's fanatics devote themselves to death to America and seek nuclear weapons to do just that. They have murdered and maimed more of our citizens and service members than any other terrorist regime on Earth." TRUMP THREATENS 'UNPRECEDENTED' ECONOMIC CONSEQUENCES FOR ANY NATION AIDING IRAN Just hours before Bessent spoke, Iran’s currency, the rial, plunged to an all-time low. The rial fell to 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar. Iranians are struggling to afford basic goods. Jonathan Harounoff, an Iran expert and British author of Persian heritage, told Fox News Digital that "Ultimately, this pressure campaign will likely continue to cripple the regime and set the stage for perhaps yet another domestic uprising. The precise timing of such a revolt is impossible to predict." Harounoff, who has written extensively on upheavals in Iran against the clerical leadership, added, "What isn't impossible to predict is that the regime is governing brutishly over a repressed population that has endured sustained economic and social immiseration. It's only a matter of time before more protests break out, and the real question is whether international organizations like the U.N. and Western governments will choose to stand by — or tangibly support the Iranian people and actively sever any cooperation they maintain with the regime." LEAKED IRAN REPORT FINDS RECORD PUBLIC ANGER AS REGIME FOCUSES ON HOLDING POWER He warned that, "Too often, outsiders speak of regime change as if it were a passive exercise. Certainly, only the people of Iran can bring about organic, homegrown, transformational change — and they have 47 years of turmoil and repression driving them toward it. But there are real ways to support the Iranian people (Starlink, supporting think tanks and foundations, raising awareness of the plight of Iranians, etc.) and help them achieve what has, until now, been a quixotic dream." Jason Brodsky, policy director at United Against Nuclear Iran (UANI), told Fox News Digital that "The question is often asked what makes this iteration of the maximum pressure campaign different from all other iterations? The answer is this iteration is taking place against a backdrop where there is a synchronization of economic and military pressure against the Iranian regime — a combination which has never been deployed by a U.S. administration until now. The U.S. naval blockade currently in place against Tehran is unprecedented. The Iranian regime's industrial base — for example, steel plants — has also been damaged following kinetic strikes. The Iranian regime’s military capacity has likewise been degraded." IRAN ACCELERATES EXECUTION CAMPAIGN AGAINST ANTI-REGIME ACTIVISTS AMID INTERNET CENSORSHIP He noted that "So Operation Economic Outcast is being launched at a time of true weakness in terms of its national power. The regime's risk tolerance may be increasing, but so is its desperation. The drivers pushing the Iranian people into the streets to protest have only gotten worse since January — with political, economic and social forces all deteriorating. The regime is seeking to use the tussle over the Strait of Hormuz as a distraction from all of this." Alireza Nader, an independent Iran expert, however, expressed skepticism that the tightening of the economic screws could provoke a mass revolt. "I don’t think starving the civilian population in Iran will lead to an American victory. The regime has demonstrated an extreme brutality toward the population, having massacred thousands of unarmed protestors this past January. And Iranians are less likely to rise up when the promised help to them from Trump and Netanyahu never materialized." Nader said that" The Woman, Life, Freedom movement against the regime prior to the war had the best chance of overthrowing the regime. This war has disrupted the Iranian people’s struggle for freedom." Beni Sabti, an Iran expert at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) in Israel, told Fox News Digital "that "there are some protests inside Iran for pensioners and those who did not get their salaries." He said the January protests began with "economic problems." articles.title: Highland Council tourist tax of £5 a night could raise £9.5m a year
articles.summary: Councillors have agreed to hold a consultation on proposals to introduce the visitor levy.
articles.body:
Highland Council is to hold a public consultation on its plans for a £5 per room, per night visitor levy for stays in hotels, B&Bs and short-term lets.

The proposed charge for hostels and campsites would be £2 per night.

A meeting of the full council in Inverness heard that the local authority had been discussing a proposed tourist tax for seven years.

Councillors were told that if the fixed-rate visitor levy went ahead it could raise about £9.5m a year to help pay for infrastructure such as roads.

Under the plans, the charges would apply across the whole Highland Council area for nine months of the year, excluding December, January and February.

Accommodation providers would retain 5% of the levy collected to help cover administration costs.

Research suggests the Highlands has almost 9.4 million annual visitors.

Council leader and SNP councillor, Raymond Bremner, said the local authority had been "labouring" at trying to introduce a charge for "a long time".

He said "most people" in the Highlands supported the idea of a levy, and he put forward a motion backing a public consultation.

Scottish Green Party councillor Chris Ballance said the charges could generate much-needed money for social housing, but he had concerns the levy would hit lower income families visiting the Highlands more than those able to afford luxury accommodation.

Liberal Democrat councillors tabled an amendment requesting that it be made clear that Highland residents would not pay the fees if visiting another part of the region.

They said residents should not be expected to pay an additional "tax", and it would also avoid a situation where people travelling for hospital appointments in Inverness having to claim expenses from NHS Highland.

Scottish Conservative councillors put forward an amendment calling for a decision on the consultation to be delayed until the results of an independent economic impact assessment were known in the coming weeks.

They said the assessment could show a negative impact on tourist visits and a potential legal challenge from tourism businesses.

Both amendments failed to get enough support and the motion was voted through.

Raymond Bremner said the council would encourage as wide a consultation as possible.

The Association of Scotland's Self-Caterers said the proposed tiered fixed rate was simpler than Highland Council's original plan for a percentage-based levy.

But the association's chief executive Fiona Campbell said councillors should have waited for the results of an independent economic impact assessment before agreeing to consult.

"Businesses and communities deserve to see the full picture of what this levy could mean before they're asked to make an informed judgement," she said.

Before the meeting, the Highland Hotel Association (HHA) said £5 was too high and suggested a lower rate of £3.

HHA said its data suggested summer occupancy rates across the region have dropped by 10% compared to last year, while costs for the sector continue to rise.

HHA chairman Craig Ewan said: "Our message to Highland Council is clear: it is not 'no' to a visitor levy, but 'not now'.

"The industry is battling a perfect storm of soaring operating costs and weakening demand."

Edinburgh was the first city in Scotland to introduce a tourist tax earlier this summer.

People staying overnight in hotels, bed and breakfasts and self-catering accommodation are charged an additional 5% on top of their original booking.

It is expected to raise about £50m annually, which could be used to fund new housing, cultural initiatives and a wider police presence.

A similar 5% levy is due to come into force in Glasgow from January 2027, while in Aberdeen a 7% charge will be introduced in April 2027 at the earliest.

The Scottish Borders, Dumfries and Galloway, Orkney and Shetland have rejected proposals for a visitor levy.
